#6183. United Airlines CEO Says “The Lead That We Have Is Going To Grow” In Thanksgiving Message To Employees

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby used his Thanksgiving message to thank employees working over the holiday and repeat his conviction that United is the best airline in the world. But his most revealing comment concerned what comes next: he expects United to widen its lead over every other airline.

In a video filmed at San Francisco International Airport and shared with Live And Let’s Fly, Kirby acknowledged the employees who will spend the holiday taking care of travelers rather than celebrating with their own families.

He also described hearing regularly from customers about employees who made their journeys easier or did something special for them. That was the most predictable and customary part of a Thanksgiving message, though Kirby could not resist adding a competitive prediction.

Kirby again called United the best airline in the world, then told employees:

“I know we’re going to keep that up in the years to come and the lead that we have is going to grow versus all of the other airlines.”

That is quite a statement, particularly the reference to all other airlines rather than just American or Delta.

I increasingly enjoy flying United. I recently wrote about how Starlink influences which flights I book, and my experiences with the crews and operation have generally been very positive too. Even as a free agent, I find myself drawn back to United. That is a good position for an airline to be in: winning my business because I like the flight it offers rather than because I need another qualifying dollar toward elite status.

But calling United the best airline in the world remains a much broader claim than I would make. My recent Air France A350 business class flight, for example, offered a level of comfort and dining that United would struggle to match consistently.

United also still has a wide variation in its onboard product. An A321neo with Starlink and a comfortable cabin presents a very different experience from an older aircraft with unreliable internet.

We can all understand why Kirby speaks this way to employees. He wants them to take pride in the airline and believe that their work is building something better. But the claim becomes more persuasive when passengers can board any aircraft in the fleet and reasonably expect a similarly good experience. That may be coming, but United is still quite a ways off.

What I appreciated most was Kirby’s emphasis on the individual employees who make travel easier.

A new cabin or faster internet can influence which flight I book. The way an employee treats me often determines how I feel about that flight afterward and critically to airlines, whether I would recommend it to others (part of the NPS score)

That becomes especially apparent when something goes wrong. A delay is frustrating, but an empathetic employee can preserve a lot of goodwill. Being ignored or brushed aside can turn an ordinary disruption into a reason to book another airline next time, which is a frequent issue for me on American Airlines.

Kirby says customers tell him about those positive encounters, including on the flight he took that day. It also connects with his recent message after the FAA ground stop, when he highlighted a crew helping a mother traveling with three young children. These are the experiences passengers remember, sometimes long after they have forgotten what they ate or which aircraft operated the flight.

Happy Thanksgiving everyone! At United, we’re about connecting people and uniting the world and that’s never more true than over the Thanksgiving holiday when we’re about to have our two busiest days of the travel period. I know many of you are going be working hard at the holidays and missing time with your friends and family so I want to say thank you for doing that and really taking care of our customer during this important time.

As we enter the Thanksgiving holiday, I’m thankful for an awful lot of things in my personal life but in my professional life, I’m thankful for all that you have done in the last several years to make United Airlines the best airline in the world. I fly a lot, including on my flight today, customers constantly are telling me stories about what a flight attendant or a pilot or a gate agent has done to ease their travel to do something special for them that makes a memory for them. So thank you for all you’ve done in the past several years to vault us to a leadership position.

Thank you for everything you’re doing right now during the holidays to take care of customers and I know we’re going to keep that up in the years to come and the lead that we have is going to grow versus all of the other airlines. Thank you for really doing things to not just make United Airlines the best in the world but to set a new standard for what it means to be a great airline in global aviation. Happy Thanksgiving and thank you.

Kirby is thankful for the employees who he believes have made United the best airline in the world, and he expects its lead over competitors to grow.

I share his enthusiasm for much of what United is doing, though I am not ready to award it that title. The more compelling part of his message was the recognition that employees earn customer loyalty through the way they treat people.

United has given me plenty of reasons to return lately. Continuing to deliver those good experiences will do far more to persuade me than any declaration that it is already the best. To everyone working at the airport or onboard today, thank you. I hope passengers remember that the person helping them get home may be spending the holiday away from their own family.

#6181. These incoming members of Congress have been here before

Rep.-elect Chris Rabb, D-Pa., greets current members of Congress in the Capitol on Nov. 11. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

“I said, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

“My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he said.

During his time in the state legislature starting in 2017, Rabb “fell in love with public service, despite the vitriol.” Now, the democratic socialist describes coming to Congress as “surreal,” as he succeeds retiring Rep. Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

Unlike some in the 100-plus-strong freshman class, they already know their way around the hallways. And Rabb has some advice for his new colleagues: “Treat your staff well. Take care of your staff; they’ll take care of you.”

Here are some of the former staffers who will join the House in January.

A couple years ago, Killin was working as chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff. But she started out on the Hill.

“It is helpful to know, as I joke, where the bathrooms are, but I still feel like I have a lot to learn,” said the Army veteran, who unseated Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in a Colorado Springs-area district.

She served as the top staffer for three House Democrats: Donna Shalala of Florida, Carolyn Maloney of New York and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.

“I’ve actually opened up two freshman offices, so it’s helpful to have done that before,” Killin said.

White will be just the third person in modern times to hold the job of nonvoting D.C. delegate. He replaces retiring Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton — also his former boss.

Before his time on the D.C. Council, he worked as her legislative counsel, watching her navigate a role with limited power in her perennial fight for statehood.

“I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he said, vowing to continue the quest for full representation even as President Donald Trump seeks to exert more control over the District.

One of just a few Republican women in the freshman class, Gruters said she “never in a million years” imagined coming to Congress herself, despite her years as a staffer.

She will replace retiring Rep. Vern Buchanan in Florida’s 16th District, after once serving as his operations director. She also worked as district director for Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla.

“I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Gruters, whose husband leads the Republican National Committee.

Rogers added another title to his résumé last week: freshman class president.

His fellow incoming Republicans tapped him for the role. Not so long ago, he was working for the Senate Judiciary Committee, fresh off a stint at the white-shoe law firm White & Case.

In 2025 he served as general counsel for Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and plans to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are currently selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers said, describing it as “deplorable.”

Rogers will succeed retiring GOP Rep. Neal Dunn in the Florida Panhandle.

García’s run for her boss’s seat drew controversy from the start. When Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., waited to publicly announce his retirement until after the filing deadline in Illinois had already passed, critics blasted him for effectively boxing out other candidates and clearing the way for his chief of staff.

He faced a rare formal disapproval vote in the House over the move. But García has insisted she is more than a hand-picked successor, saying on her campaign website that she has “delivered solutions rooted in lived experience.”

The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech company Oracle.

He also worked as campaign manager for Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, earning an endorsement from the retiring longtime Democrat and campaign cash from groups aligned with him.

Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

Sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

Once a precocious child magician who wrote his own book of tricks, Lasher also got an early start in politics.

“I feel supremely fortunate to have wandered into Jerry Nadler’s political orbit as a teenager 30 years ago, and then to have worked in his congressional office a decade later,” Lasher wrote in an opinion piece for City & State New York.

Backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of big names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

Villegas ousted GOP Rep. David Valadao in a closely watched race in the San Joaquin Valley.

A decade ago, he was an intern for Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif. And the progressive also interned for former California state Rep. Rudy Salas, who made unsuccessful bids to unseat Valadao in 2022 and 2024.

A San Diego City councilmember, Von Wilpert flipped the seat held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who decided not to run for reelection under a map redrawn by Democrats.

When she worked for the National Labor Relations Board in 2016, she was detailed to the House Education and Labor Committee, working under ranking member Robert C. Scott, D-Va.

#6180. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

#6179. A Thanksgiving Resolution

The boy grew into a man and his eyes were opened to the world around him, to the beauty of nature, the sights and smells of the world’s great cities, and the elegance of the human race. But he noticed something else, something troubling.

Humanity, for all its hints of goodness, was inimitably at war with itself. Not just wars of weaponry and nation states, but deeper wars of ideas and values. Like a cancer imperfectly treated, the pestilence of irreconcilable division ebbed and flowed…but perpetually manifested itself in fierce battles and spilled blood.

The man took this all in, wondering where his place was in all this was. A humanitarian? A missionary? A soldier? A politician? A writer? A peacemaker? Perhaps a little of each. Perhaps none of the above. He married a woman from a different culture and with a different worldview. The challenge of marriage personified the challenge of the surrounding world — putting differences asides to build trust, loyalty, and respect while growing in love and patience. Was this even possible absent divine intervention?

Then one Thanksgiving Day it hit him. He could not change the world. Not alone anyway. But there was one one thing he could do, something so trite on the one hand but absolutely revolutionary on the other: he could love his neighbor as he loved himself.

Just how would that look? Being honest, generous, forgiving, joyful, peaceful, patient, kind, and faithful to everyone he encountered. He would often fail, but it became a primary goal in life.

The man still ponders his place in this world, but there is one thing he knows — there may be many things he is not, but he is a traveler and that gives him a unique opportunity to put his maxim to practice in venues far beyond the friendly confines of home. Blessed with so much through circumstance of birth, he pauses to reflect upon the blessings he has been the recipient of, many from those who follow a similar maxim.

Perhaps one day you will meet him and he can encourage you or share in your struggles. His goal is to leave every person he crosses paths with knowing that they are loved and respected. Life is often unkind and this goal is insurmountable in all places and at all times, but it is worth pursuing.

Now, he invites you to join him in his journey to put others before himself. One day and one person at a time, humanity can tame the inhumane world it finds itself in.

This post has appeared annually on Thanksgiving Day since 2015.

#6178. Qatar Airways Promo Code: 25% Off for Black Friday

Before a trip, one of the first big decisions you have to make is how to get there. Picking the right airline can be difficult, especially when there are so many choices to consider, and prices are constantly fluctuating. One wonderfully chic option is Qatar Airways, which operates in dozens of cities across the world, from the Middle East to the Americas to Australia. Known for its exceptional business class and luxury service, this is the airline to choose if you want a premium experience before you even set foot in your travel destination. Whether you’re taking a bucket-list trip to Doha or want to jazz up an annual vacation to Paris, Qatar Airways lets you enhance what can sometimes be the most stressful and dreary part of travel. Below, find all the best promo codes and coupons to help you save while enjoying the high life this Black Friday weekend.

Hurry, these Black Friday sales won't last long: Through end of day November 29 (11:59pm ET), find economy and business class flights up to 25% off for travel through October 31, 2027. Flights purchased in the sale are flexible too, with one free date change if needed. As for the fine print, there are some blackout dates, and the minimum stay is seven days.

Beyond the Cyber Week discounts, you can find Qatar Airways flash sales directly on the website, which run on and off throughout the year. You’ll need to catch them at just the right time (subscribing to the newsletter will help ensure you don’t miss any updates), since, due to their nature, they’re gone in a flash. The current sale is offering up to 15% off fares for flights to 170+ destinations for trips occurring through March 22, 2027. But you’ll have to book quickly since flash sales come and go in the blink of an eye.

Are you a student between the ages of 18 and 30 enrolled at an accredited college or university? Traveling back and forth between school and home can be pricey, but thanks to Qatar Airways Student Club, you can visit family during holidays or travel for your studies without breaking the bank. Expect a plethora of spectacular benefits you’ll want to take advantage of, including complimentary Wi-Fi in the sky, extra baggage allowance (22 pounds of additional luggage, or an extra bag, depending on your route—especially helpful for beginning or end of semester flights), and an upgrade to a higher Privilege Club tier if you fly as a Student Club member at least once a year. You’ll also get 10% off your first flight, 15% off your second, and 20% off your third and fourth, as well as two complimentary date changes for your flights. Perhaps the most exciting benefit of all (especially for those of us, like me, who are no longer students), those enrolled in the Student Club can invite up to three family members or friends to be Student Companions, so they’ll share all of the Student Club benefits on their trip.

Join the Privilege Club, Qatar Airways's loyalty program, to rake in tons of benefits. Those who join now can use the code PCAMER26 by December 31, 2026, to earn up to 4,000 bonus Avios (Qatar Airways’s rewards currency) to use on upcoming flights, upgrades, and extra baggage allowances. Travelers will receive their Avios directly in their online account after their first flight as a member, as long as they remember to include their membership number when booking their original flight. Plus, members can take full advantage of Qatar Airways’ excellent business class by using Avios to upgrade from Economy. There are occasionally Business Class promo codes during seasonal sales with direct fare discounts that guests should keep an eye out for. Guests can also combine Avios with cash to purchase flight fare, so no matter how small your balance of Avios, you can still use them at any time.

It’s free to sign up for the Privilege Club, which features four tiers of benefits. The Burgundy tier is the entry-level option, which offers 10% off seat selection and the ability to earn Avios to redeem on future flights, upgrades, or baggage allowances. To move to higher tiers and reap further rewards like priority check-in, lounge access, and extra baggage allowances, guests will need to earn Qpoints by booking flights, shopping at Qatar’s Hamad International Airport, booking vacation packages through Qatar Airways Holidays, or signing up and spending with the Qatar Airways Privilege Club Credit Card by Doha Bank. To jump to the Silver tier, travelers will need 150 Qpoints. To upgrade to Gold, they’ll need 300 Qpoints, and 600 for Platinum status.

Privilege Club members also get access to a whole host of offers that aren’t available to anyone else, including a current offer for up to 12% off flights when booked on Qatar Airways’ website or app with a Qatar Airways Privilege Club Credit Card. Be sure to use the promo code QRPCFLIGHT when booking with Qatar Airways to score this deal. The offer is available for bookings made through April 30, 2027.

One of the best ways to upgrade your tier level is by keeping an eye out for “Double Qpoints” promotions. They’ll pop up on Qatar Airways’ offers page, and will help travelers earn Silver, Gold, or Platinum status faster. With higher tiers come better benefits, meaning you’re one step closer to lazing away in a premium lounge with your complimentary extra baggage space. This is only applicable to Privilege Club members, so it’s worth signing up for free before booking that last-minute flight to London, or a long-haul ticket to Mumbai.

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6175. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister currently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

In a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he said when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he said, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with plans to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a company registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s company, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he said, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

#6174. Two Surprisingly Delicious Meals In Singapore Airlines Economy Class

First, a note on the trip. What a trip it was! I never wrote a full trip report and it is far too late now, but I flew for almost three days without stopping…22,880 miles to be exact from LAX-HNL-MAJ-KWA-KSA-PNI-TKK-GUM-NRT/HND-SIN-RGN-BKK-LHR-JFK-PHL.

I enjoyed many meals on the trip, including a mix of economy class and business class, but if I had to pick a favorite, it was breakfast on Singapore Airlines in economy class from Tokyo Narita to Singapore Changi.

The 7 hour flight took off just before midnight. I was expecting a large meal after takeoff and a snack prior to landing, but the opposite occurred. Shortly after takeoff, FAs offered a chicken wrap with choice of beverage. Singapore Airlines offers its signature Singapore Sling cocktails even in economy class, which was a tad too sweet but decent. The wrap was surprisingly good, with very fresh ingredients.

Singapore also uses “real” cutlery in economy class:

No menus were distributed, so I figured that would be it for meal service. But two hours prior to landing FAs served a hot breakfast. I chose a cheese omelet and was very pleasantly surprised at how nice it turned out. It was fluffy, nicely seasoned, and the side of cooked tomato, potatoes and bacon hit the spot. Breakfast was served with orange juice, coffee, a muffin, fresh fruit, and a bread roll.

If all Singapore flights have food like this one, at least you won’t have to worry about bringing your own food when flying in Singapore Airlines economy class.

My Meal of the Week feature examines an airline meal from my travels over the years. This may be a meal from earlier in the week or it may be a meal served over a decade ago.

#6173. Norse Atlantic Cancels All Flights As Norwegian Operating Company Files For Bankruptcy

Norse Atlantic has canceled all flights and stopped selling tickets after its Norwegian operating company decided to file for bankruptcy. Efforts to save the remaining business continue, but for passengers with upcoming bookings, the immediate reality is grim. Another airline built around affordable longhaul travel has run out of money, further calling into question the sustainability of the low-cost business model.

Norse Atlantic announced today, November 27, 2026, that the board of its Norwegian operating subsidiary, Norse Atlantic Airways AS, will file bankruptcy petition with the Agder District Court in Norway.

The company could not secure sufficient funding to meet its immediate cash needs. Its board concluded that continued operations at the Norwegian subsidiary were no longer viable. The publicly listed parent, Norse Atlantic ASA, and other group companies are outside this filing. Management is still seeking a solution for the remaining business, including the UK and USA subsidiaries.

But all flights are canceled and ticket sales have ended. CEO Eivind Roald said:

“We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners.”

The bankruptcy announcement followed another serious development earlier today.

According to Reuters, the lessors of all 12 aircraft in the Norse fleet sent notices terminating their lease agreements. Norse disputes the validity of those notices.

That leaves the remaining business facing an enormous challenge. Finding new financing is difficult enough. Resolving access to the aircraft needed to operate the airline adds another obstacle.

The deterioration has been rapid. On November 25, Norse warned that its financial situation was critical. It suspended flights the following day. Today came the lease termination disclosures and the decision to put the Norwegian operating company into bankruptcy.

I’m not optimistic about this carrier ever flying again.

When I first wrote about Norse in 2021, I welcomed the prospect of another airline offering inexpensive transatlantic flights after Norwegian abandoned longhaul service.

My enthusiasm was primarily about competition. Even travelers who never booked Norwegian benefited when its fares forced larger airlines to respond. I hoped Norse could provide similar pressure while avoiding the problems that had undermined Norwegian.

Earlier this year, I covered Norse withdrawing from Los Angeles as fuel costs surged. Cutting routes that could no longer support themselves seemed sensible, even as it raised concerns about how much room the airline had left to maneuver.

Reuters identifies soaring fuel costs associated with the Iran war as a major pressure on the business. That is a brutal challenge for an airline trying to sell inexpensive tickets on flights that spend many hours in the air. World’s “most famous” flight attendant, Sara Nelson, a Marxist who seemingly aspires to higher office herself, blamed the Iran war:

On Thanksgiving, the war with Iran means U.S. based @afacwa Flight Attendants, and all Norse Atlantic workers, are facing losing their careers. All flights are suspended. Crew are traveling home w/ livelihoods hanging in the balance. @ITFglobalunion https://t.co/x7SDrvL5DI

— Sara Nelson (@FlyingWithSara) November 26, 2026

But the broader difficulty with this model remains. A low advertised fare can fill seats without producing enough revenue to sustain the operation. Charging separately for meals and bags helps, but the airline simply could not sustain fares high enough to break even.

Established network carriers have advantages that are difficult to replicate, including connecting traffic and customers willing to pay substantial premiums for flexible schedules or premium cabins.

If you have an upcoming Norse booking, the airline has confirmed that all flights are canceled. If you’re left with a cancelling itinerary, contact your card issuer about the options available for a canceled service (if you paid extra for travel insurance, you can start there). If you booked through a travel agency or as part of a package, contact that provider too.

There will be plenty of people saying this outcome was predictable. Indeed it was, but that offers little comfort to employees facing uncertainty or passengers whose plans have fallen apart.

Norse gave travelers another option. Losing that option is disappointing even for those of us who generally preferred to fly on other carriers. I hope something viable can emerge from the remaining business. But another temporary infusion of cash into an operation that will soon need the same help again would be foolishness.

Norse Atlantic has canceled all flights and ended ticket sales as its Norwegian operating subsidiary moves to file for bankruptcy. The parent company and UK business remain outside that filing, with efforts to secure a future continuing.

For now, passengers need alternative travel arrangements, and employees face an uncertain future. I welcomed Norse because more competition benefits travelers. I am sorry to see it reach this point, even if the warning signs have been visible for some time.

#6171. Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

That means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

There’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, said Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

“Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres said.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the new year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

“There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

In addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

“There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”

“I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

“We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet announced — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin said.

#6170. Cathay Pacific Joins Chase Ultimate Rewards Then Raises Partner Award Prices A Week Later

Cathay Pacific became a Chase Ultimate Rewards transfer partner on November 18. One week later, it announced that selected partner award tickets will cost more Asia Miles beginning in January. As much as I celebrate the addition of Cathay Pacific to Chase, the timing offers a useful reminder: the value of flexible points depends on what you can actually book with them.

Cathay Pacific has announced higher mileage requirements for selected airline partner awards ticketed beginning January 5, 2027. The increases vary by route and cabin. Several of the published examples rise by 20%, while some longhaul business class awards increase by roughly 8% (see my table below).

Cathay is also eliminating Companion Ticket Awards from the same date. Standard Awards and Upgrade Awards on Cathay Pacific itself are unaffected by this announcement. The separate oneworld multi-carrier award chart is also unchanged.

VFTW highlights the increases, including the following examples shared by Cathay.

These are one-way prices per passenger and represent selected changes rather than a complete new partner award chart:

For example, British Airways first class from Los Angeles to London will increase from 135,000 to 162,000 Asia Miles. For two passengers, that is another 54,000 miles for the same one-way journey…

That is a substantial increase, especially when taxes and surcharges are still payable in addition to the miles (book BA with JAL miles to avoid the surcharges).

Cathay attributes the changes to higher costs charged by its partner airlines. I understand that redeeming miles for a seat on another carrier involves an expense for the program, though it is also my understanding that partners actually pay very little for out of pocket for these seats (see this OMAAT post).

Chase added Cathay Pacific as a transfer partner on November 18, with eligible Ultimate Rewards points transferring to Asia Miles at a 1:1 ratio, a positive development for Chase cardholders.

More ways to compare award prices and access seats are useful, and this devaluation does not erase the value of having Cathay available. Still, announcing higher partner award prices a week later takes some of the shine off the news (not that I am claiming any collusion!).

Someone who saw the new transfer option and moved points into Asia Miles without a particular redemption in mind now has a deadline to consider: it is exactly why I do not transfer points unless I am ready to immediately book.

A bank point that can become miles in several programs gives you options. Once transferred, it becomes subject to the pricing and availability of the receiving program.

That flexibility has value. I say this often, but keep your points flexible as long as you can.

Perhaps Asia Miles offers the best deal today. By the time you are ready to book, another program may offer a lower price or access to a more convenient flight. Keeping the points in a flexible currency account like Chase Ultimate Rewards allows you to make that comparison when it actually matters.

Of course, there are circumstances in which a transfer bonus or a specific booking opportunity makes moving points worthwhile, but it has to be very compelling if I’m going to move points over without booking.

Cathay says the current mileage requirements remain available for tickets issued through January 4, 2027, at 11:59 pm Hong Kong time (for U.S. readers, that is 10:59 AM Eastern).  The deadline concerns when the ticket is issued, rather than when you travel. You can book a later trip at the current price if award space is available and the ticket is issued before the cutoff.

Cathay also says date changes to those tickets can retain the original mileage requirement after the increase, subject to award availability and applicable change fees. Other changes will be subject to the revised mileage requirements.

I appreciate the advance notice very much. If you have a trip in mind and find the seats, there is an opportunity to act before the increase.

Cathay Pacific is increasing selected partner award prices beginning January 5, 2027, shortly after becoming a Chase Ultimate Rewards transfer partner.

The Chase addition remains welcome, and Cathay-operated Standard Awards are unaffected by this announcement. But the higher partner prices make some redemptions less attractive. This news once again reinforces the value of keeping bank points flexible until I am ready to book…don’t transfer until you are ready to book.

#6166. Review: United Airlines 737 MAX 8 Economy Class Newark To Nuuk, Greenland

My United Airlines flight from Newark to Nuuk, Greenland featured a friendly crew, two meal services, and a spectacular approach onboard a Boeing 737 MAX 8 in economy class. Economy Plus was perfectly comfortable for the four-hour daytime journey, though the flight became much fuller than I had expected thanks to a large contingent of United employees taking advantage of their travel benefits.

Greenland had been on my bucket list for years, and United’s nonstop service from Newark offered an opportunity to finally visit. I was heading back to Germany to pick up my children after their summer visit with family and decided to take a rather scenic route via Nuuk and Copenhagen.

I had already traveled from Palm Springs through San Francisco and Denver to reach Newark. By the time I boarded this flight, I was tired…but very excited about what lay ahead.

I booked the entire United itinerary from Palm Springs to Nuuk using 40,000 Air Canada Aeroplan points, plus $5.60 in government taxes and the CAD39 partner booking fee.

A cash ticket for the itinerary was about $1,600, so I was pleased to use miles instead. The premium cabin on the Greenland flight, marketed as Premium Plus, was sold out when I booked (and I don’t mean no saver partner award space, but sold out completely).

My overnight flight from Denver arrived at the A Gates, and the Nuuk flight would depart from the same terminal.

There was a United Club nearby, but I wanted a shower and barista-made coffee, so I took the airside shuttle bus to Terminal C and visited the United Club near gate C123. I wrote separately about that visit. There was no wait for a shower, and although I would have preferred hotter water and stronger pressure, it was refreshing to clean up after the redeye.

An illy double-shot cappuccino helped too. I had breakfast, got some work done, and then returned by bus to the A Gates about 30 minutes before boarding.

This turned out to be a much more energetic flight than I expected.

The night before departure, the flight appeared less than half full. By the time we pushed back a few minutes late, it was much closer to capacity, with a large number of United employees traveling on standby.

I initially had an Economy Plus row to myself, but two jovial United employees joined me. They were heading to Greenland for just one night. As I explained in my first impressions of the flight, several employees described arriving in Nuuk, exploring town, taking a twilight boat excursion, and visiting a bar before returning to the airport for the morning flight back to Newark.

That sounded absolutely exhausting to me, but I understood the appeal. If I had those travel benefits, I would certainly be tempted to use them on a route like this! There was certainly a festive atmosphere onboard, and I enjoyed hearing how others planned to spend their short time in Greenland.

Boarding was delayed 20 minutes, but it was finally time to step onboard.

I was warmly greeted by Craig, the purser, as I boarded. More on him below.

United’s 737 MAX 8 features 150 seats one economy class in a 3-3 configuration. Seats are Collins Meridian slimline seats and feature an adjustable headrest and seatback screens. Legroom is 30 inches (34 inches in Economy Plus), the seat is 17 inches wide, and seats recline two inches.

I selected a window seat on the left side of the aircraft in Economy Plus.

There are individual air nozzles onboard as well as seatback power (A/C under the seat and both USB-A and USB-C under the screen).

The window seat on the A side proved an excellent choice during our approach, though the best side will depend on which direction the aircraft lands, which will depend on the winds.

Despite a flight time of only about four hours, there were two services during the flight.

I had ordered United’s “balanced diet” special meal, which consisted of chicken pieces in tomato sauce accompanied by a side salad, bread roll, and “That’s It” fruit snack for dessert. It was not exactly gourmet, but it did the job and I had some club soda to drink with it.

The regular choices for passengers were pasta or beef. Is the diet meal worth ordering?

As we approached Nuuk, I received an Indian vegetarian wrap (other passengers received a pizza pocket). It was not necessary for such a short flight, but appreciated nevertheless. I enjoyed a cup of illy coffee as well.

United’s seatback screens feature a deep content of movies and TV shows with a handful of game and audio options. The same library of content was also available via streaming to your own device.

Complimentary earphones were provided, though you could pair your own device to these screens, which I did.

The flight featured Viasat Wi-Fi, available for purchase for $10 ($8 for MileagePlus members) and it worked well over the Atlantic.

United’s 737 MAX 8 has one lavatory in the front for premium cabin passengers and two in the back for economy class, which is not a great proportion.

The purser, Craig, was a highlight of the flight.

Apparently, he worked nearly every Nuuk flight that summer and has become something of an institution on the route. He was friendly, professional, and knowledgeable, making his way through the cabin and chatting with passengers.

We had a nice conversation about restaurant recommendations in Nuuk. I appreciated speaking with someone who knew the destination and could offer advice before I arrived. What a fun assignment to spend the summer flying to Greenland!

A good crew can make an ordinary flight enjoyable, and Craig helped make this unusual route feel even more special. Between the enthusiastic employee travelers and his warm welcome, the mood onboard was very pleasant.

I had chosen an “A” window seat on the port side, which gave me a northerly view during our final approach. Aircraft can arrive from the opposite direction depending on the wind, so the view will vary, but I was very happy with my choice.

As we descended below the clouds, tundra and floating ice came into view. Then the sun broke through, revealing the mountainous landscape around Nuuk.

I have flown over Greenland many times, looking down from cruising altitude and wondering what it would be like to visit. Seeing it from this perspective, knowing I would soon be on the ground, was quite different.

Some of the mountains still held snow, and the landscape looked rugged and sparsely populated. It was majestic.

I shared more photographs in my earlier post about the approach. My arrival in the Faroe Islands a couple of years earlier may have been even more scenic, but this was nevertheless a wonderful welcome to Greenland.

This is a flight where I would strongly recommend a window seat.

We landed at 7:08 pm local time under clear skies and taxied to a parking position outside the terminal.

Air Greenland-branded stairs were brought to the aircraft, and we walked down onto the apron. It was about 55ºF outside…crisp, clear, and beautiful.

After the long journey from Southern California, I was finally in Greenland.

Next came immigration, which turned out to be a story of its own.

> Read More: My Longest EES Immigration Wait Yet Was In Tiny Nuuk, Greenland

This was such a fun flight. Economy Plus was comfortable for the relatively short daytime journey, Craig provided excellent service, and the atmosphere onboard was cheerful…it almost felt like an inaugural flight. The approach into Nuuk was the highlight and made me very glad I had selected a window seat on the A side (though again, I was fortunate because the approaches change based on prevailing wind conditions).

Getting to Newark had required several flights and an overnight journey from Denver, but this final segment was a pleasure. I was thrilled to finally reach Greenland and appreciated being able to do so on United.

#6165. Latino Democrats celebrate midterm gains, with warning for party

California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

But California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

“Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, said House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

“While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he said.

Leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

California Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very issue that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

“Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she said. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

“A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido said. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”

Several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he said.

The candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez said. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”

Amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

“The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto said.

Deals and pricing updated as of 5:06 p.m. on November 27, 2026.

It's that time of year again: Holiday gift-giving is on the mind, travelers are planning 2027 (and last-minute 2026) trips, and Black Friday hotel deals are in full swing. Those looking to score the best bang for their buck on hotel deals this year will find that there are already tons of excellent offers from some of your favorite brands, whether you're looking for a beachy Caribbean escape or a ski vacation in Aspen. Are you the type of person who stays loyal to their favorite brands, like World of Hyatt and Marriott Bonvoy? Or more the traveler who enjoys scrolling through endless options on travel booking sites like Expedia and Booking.com? Whatever your method, there are tons of ways to save.

This Black Friday, many hotels are offering generous discounts, reward point bonuses, complimentary amenities, and flexible travel windows that will allow you to plan well into 2027. These limited-time holiday savings will let you elevate your upcoming getaways while staying within your budget, making this one of the smartest times to plan next year’s vacation. #6160. Steep 2026 Travel Tuesday Deals Are Already Rolling In

Deals and pricing updated as of 5:31 p.m. on November 27, 2026.

Black Friday might be wrapping up, but I’m not ready to close the suitcase—or the sale tabs—just yet. If you’ve been tossing around ideas for a winter escape, a long-awaited European summer, or that big trip you keep saying you’ll book someday, now’s a better time than ever to start looking (and booking).

The early offers cover quite a bit of ground, from all-inclusive resorts in the Caribbean and far-flung cruise itineraries to guided adventures, discounted tours, and car rentals for the road ahead. Some deals are short-term, others run through Travel Tuesday, and most have booking windows that are worth catching before they disappear. I’m keeping this list updated as new promotions come in, with all the details you need to know before you book.

Read on for 21 of the best Travel Tuesday deals available right now.

Where the pool is ready and the palm trees sway at JW Marriott Orlando Bonnet Creek Resort & Spa

The offer applies to stays taken between November 29, 2026, and May 2, 2027, so you’ll be able to take your pick from a fun winter weekend, spring break, or early-summer getaway.

There’s plenty of inspiration across the portfolio, too, from family-friendly desert adventures at JW Marriott Tucson Starr Pass Resort and Spa and the newly transformed oceanfront Mauna Kea Beach Hotel, Autograph Collection, to a playful city stay at Moxy Halifax Downtown, an art-filled New Orleans retreat at Renaissance New Orleans Arts Warehouse District Hotel, or a lively Nashville weekend at W Nashville.

Select hotels in these destinations include breakfast too. Just note that advance-booking requirements and minimum stays vary by property, so check the offer terms before confirming your plans. Not a Hilton Honors member? Joining is simple and free!

You can save at a sweet glamping site with Under Canvas's early Travel Tuesday discounts.

Save on Sandals Saint Vincent and The Grenadines—the perfect sanctuary for relaxation within over 50 acres of breathtaking Jurassic Park–like scenery.

Delta Air Lines and American Express offer seven cobranded cards for everyone from occasional Delta flyers to frequent travelers.

Depending on the card and the offer you qualify for, you could earn thousands of bonus Delta SkyMiles.

Here’s how the current offers compare and what to consider before applying.

Apply for the : Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 125,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.

The following is a comparison of the various welcome offers currently available. Note that TPG values Delta SkyMiles at 1.2 cents per mile as of November 2026. This valuation assumes you're using your miles to book flights with Delta or one of its partners.

American Express has a few eligibility rules to keep in mind before applying for one of these cards. For starters, Amex typically only allows a person to earn one welcome bonus per card in their lifetime. That means you'll want to prioritize applying when a card offers an elevated, limited-time offer, such as the ones all but one of these cards have right now.

You also may not be eligible for a welcome bonus on a personal Delta Amex card if you have or previously had a higher-tier Delta Amex card. For example, if you have or previously had the Delta Reserve Amex, you may not be eligible for the welcome offers on the Delta Blue, the Delta Gold and the Delta Platinum.

Delta's business Amex cards are not subject to this same "family rule."

Amex may consider other factors, including your income, your credit score and your history with the issuer, when determining your eligibility. Fortunately, you'll generally find out whether you're eligible for a welcome offer before accepting the card.

Related: A complete guide to Amex's 1-bonus-per-lifetime restrictions

Delta offers four personal cards. The card that is right for you depends on how frequently you fly with Delta and how much you’re willing to pay for an annual fee.

Let’s take a look at what differentiates each of the Delta SkyMiles personal cards.

Best for: Delta loyalists or those who want Sky Club access (subject to limitations).

The is ideal for hardcore Delta fans and frequent flyers.

#6158. Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

“One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”

The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

“We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”

On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust new majority.

When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”

The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

“Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

Without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”

This report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

#6156. BermudAir Adds 10 New Destinations, 18 New Routes

Bermudian flag carrier BermudAir will nearly double its U.S. footprint next year as it launches new connections across North and Central America and the Caribbean.

The carrier announced Tuesday that it will serve New Orleans; Nashville, Tennessee; New Haven, Connecticut; Burlington, Vermont; Portland, Maine; San Antonio; New Brunswick, Canada; Ocho Rios, Jamaica; San Salvador, El Salvador; and San Pedro Sula, Honduras, for the first time.

Accompanying the 10 new destinations are 18 new routes. BermudAir is also moving to expand service to existing markets, such as Bermuda, Anguilla, Belize, Grand Cayman, Guatemala, and Turks and Caicos.

“From New Orleans and Nashville to San Antonio and New England, we’re seeing tremendous interest in what BermudAir offers,” founder and CEO Adam Scott said in a news release.

BermudAir currently serves eight U.S. cities, all on or close to the East Coast, and three destinations in Canada. Its main hub is L.F. Wade International Airport in St. George’s, Bermuda.
