#6155. Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”

“I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”

The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

“They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”

A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

“We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”

Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

She also said that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

“Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”

The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

#6154. How Much Does A Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 Engine Cost?

Allora Empire Art | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Rolls-Royce does not publish list prices for the Trent 1000, so every figure quoted for the Dreamliner engine is an estimate, and the most commonly cited is about $20 million per engine. That number answers only part of the question, because transaction prices differ from list estimates and the expense that has defined this engine’s reputation arrives years after delivery in the form of shop visits and retrofit campaigns.

A better answer therefore separates three prices: what an engine is estimated to cost at list, what a documented order implies once its fine print is read, and what it costs to keep one flying. This article works through each, then examines how Rolls-Royce’s latest upgrade could change the ownership economics.

Simple Flying’s 2025 survey of commercial engines places the Trent 1000 at an estimated $20 million, which sits below the roughly $22 million it assigns to the rival GE GEnx and well below Rolls-Royce’s own Trent 7000 at $25 million and Trent XWB at $35 million. The Trent 1000 can reach 74,411 pounds of thrust (331 kN), and the Trent 7000’s thrust band falls within that limit as well, so thrust alone does not explain the price spread. SlashGear arrives at the same $20 million figure and describes an engine optimized for the Boeing 787, with a fan that produces about 85% of the engine’s total thrust.

These figures are best read as list-price approximations rather than transaction prices, since common estimates exclude discounts, bulk purchase pricing, and support contracts. For example, Singapore Airlines had an order for 62 GE9X engines with a list value of about $45 million per engine, including a 12-year service contract. For context, narrowbody engines are not necessarily cheaper once transactions replace estimates: Willis Lease Finance purchased 15 Pratt & Whitney PW1100 engines in 2024 for $363.9 million, about $24.3 million each, more than the Trent 1000 estimate.

The clearest official data point is a January 2018 announcement in which Rolls-Royce said lessor AerCap had ordered Trent 1000 engines to power 10 Boeing 787s, a deal valued at $450 million at list prices. Dividing by 20 engines yields $22.5 million apiece, the figure usually quoted, but the arithmetic depends on assumptions the announcement does not confirm: two engines per aircraft and no spares.

A footnote in the release adds a more significant caveat, since Rolls-Royce measures its order book at list prices and, for long-term aftermarket contracts, counts the revenue it expects to recognize within seven years of the announcement. The release does not say whether such revenue sits inside the $450 million, so the $22.5 million figure may blend hardware with service value and should be treated as an upper reference for the engine itself rather than a price tag. The footnote also cautions that an order’s stated value may not reflect future revenue.

Two other details bound the interpretation, since the order covered the TEN variant, which entered service in November 2017, and AerCap held options on five more aircraft outside the stated value. The TEN draws on Trent XWB and Advance technologies and helps the Dreamliner achieve 20% greater efficiency than the aircraft it replaces, according to Rolls-Royce. Rolls-Royce also notes that the Trent 1000 powered the first flight of every Dreamliner version, the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10. Because list prices exclude negotiated discounts, the price AerCap actually paid is not disclosed in the announcement.

Tada Images | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Purchase price is only the entry fee, because Simple Flying reports that a single unscheduled shop visit can exceed $5 million once transport logistics, spare engine leasing, and teardown labor are counted. The same report says early Trent 1000s achieved time-on-wing intervals that were a fraction of the GEnx-1B benchmark of more than 20,000 operating hours before the first major shop visit, which made the interval the main driver of lifetime cost. Because the Trent 1000 is a three-shaft design built exclusively for the Dreamliner, its tooling, spare parts, and overhaul procedures are unique to it and are not shared with the GEnx fleet.

Many Rolls-Royce operators shield themselves from that volatility through TotalCare, a power-by-the-hour agreement in which the airline pays a fixed rate per flight hour and the manufacturer assumes the cost of shop visits. Such contracts convert an uncertain maintenance expense into a predictable one, though the engine’s true cost to the operator then becomes a recurring rate rather than a single purchase price. Because the fleet now spans several build standards, airlines and maintenance hubs must also manage parts inventories and tooling for each sub-generation, an overhead that TotalCare terms do not remove.

Rolls-Royce’s exposure under those agreements explains why durability failures hurt it directly: in 2019, the company said added repair costs would push a small number of its contracts into loss-making territory, which its finance chief put at around three. Those losses made up about half of an exceptional charge of about £1.4 billion expected that year.

The technical cause was corrosion-related fatigue cracking in the intermediate- and high-pressure turbine blades, which emerged within five years of the engine’s 2011 entry into service and eventually affected as many as 500 engines. Groundings peaked at close to 50 Dreamliners in 2018, and in April of that year the FAA cut extended-range twin-engine operating time for Package C aircraft from 330 minutes to 140, a restriction that complicated long trans-Pacific planning. Operators such as Air New Zealand and British Airways grounded aircraft for inspections, and several affected carriers leased older, less fuel-efficient jets to protect schedules, which added millions of dollars in operating expense.

The financial tally has grown with each update: by November 2019, Rolls-Royce put the cost of the Trent 1000 problems at £2.4 billion for 2017 through 2023, an additional £800 million, and said the TEN would need servicing every four years instead of five. Later accounts place the total above $3 billion, covering retrofits, engine modifications, and customer compensation.

The commercial damage extended beyond Rolls-Royce’s accounts, as GE secured roughly two-thirds of the in-service 787 fleet and recent widebody sales campaigns ordered 677 GEnx-powered aircraft against only 71 for the Trent 1000. Emirates President Tim Clark, citing instability in the Trent program, said in September 2019 that he would not commit to ordering 787s, an early sign that reliability concerns could cost sales as well as repair money.

The Trent XWB just keeps getting better and better.

Rolls-Royce’s answer is the Trent 1000 XE, delivered in two certified phases; the first, approved by the FAA in June 2025, introduced a high-pressure turbine blade with 40% more cooling, along with changes to the combustor, fuel spray nozzles, and controller software. Rolls-Royce says that package alone more than doubles the time on wing, and the second phase, certified in late 2025, redesigns the blade shroud and adds advanced coatings for roughly 30% more. Together, the phases are meant to triple time on wing relative to the TEN, and CEO Tufan Erginbilgiç has put the real-world figure as high as six years between shop visits for some customers. The confidence rests partly on the Trent 7000, which has flown with the same durability technology since 2022, and by mid-2026 the fleet using the new blades had accumulated almost three million engine flying hours.

Deployment is under way, since Lufthansa flew the first XE-equipped 787 in November 2025. The XE is now standard on new Trent-powered deliveries, and by early 2026, more than 50 in-service engines carried the improved blades, with a fleet-wide retrofit targeted for the end of 2027. Rolls-Royce committed to upgrading existing engines at no additional charge to airlines, and it added maintenance capacity in the UK, Germany, and Singapore worth roughly 100 more shop visits a year. LATAM Airlines has selected the XE for its 787s, a win Rolls-Royce credits to the durability gains.

The Trent 1000 work forms part of a £1 billion durability program that also covers the Trent 7000 and Trent XWB, and Rolls-Royce has raised its mid-term time-on-wing improvement target from 40% to 80% by 2027. Investors reacted by pushing Rolls-Royce shares sharply higher after the company raised its profit guidance on the back of the engine fixes.

Over the next two years, the price tag on a Trent 1000 will likely matter less than evidence of how long upgraded engines stay on wing. Once the fleet retrofit concludes, the industry will have its first fleet-scale record of shop visit intervals for the XE standard, and that record should do more than any list estimate to set how lessors and operators value the engine. Simple arithmetic shows why, since tripling the interval between visits would cut visits per flying hour to about a third, a change in lifetime economics that outweighs the small purchase price gap separating the Trent 1000 from its GE rival.

Two uncertainties remain, since the sources reviewed do not say whether the XE standard changes the purchase price of a new engine, and the headline interval claims apply to some customers rather than the whole fleet. Pricing is therefore likely to shift toward service contract terms, where Rolls-Royce can back its durability claims with guaranteed rates, and away from the hardware figure that dominates headlines. If the 2027 data confirm the promised gains, the engine’s share of new 787 orders will be the first place the market shows that it believes them.

Mendocino, a small coastal town in northern California, has welcomed its first points property. The nearly 50-year-old Hill House hotel was renovated and reopened in June 2026 as Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino, Outdoor Collection by Marriott Bonvoy — making it the first and only member of a major hotel loyalty program in Mendocino proper. (The closest options are members of IHG One Rewards and Wyndham Rewards in neighboring Fort Bragg.)

The Mendocino Coast region is known for its charming small-town vibes, natural beauty and outdoor pursuits, so the Trailborn brand’s laidback nature lodge concept fits in here like a seal in nearby Mendocino Bay. I stayed three nights in late October to get a first look at the property (and the town, which is on TPG’s 2027 Where to Go list).

Nestled just a few minutes’ walk outside downtown Mendocino, Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino’s unassuming two-story buildings fit right in with the surrounding hotel scene. The design is inspired by nature — specifically, the redwood forests and tide pools of the surrounding Mendocino Coast — while still feeling modern and polished.

The grounds are bursting with native plants, many of them still in bloom when I visited in late October. Botanical art prints and zoological illustrations on the walls give a nod to the great outdoors, and curious guests can lose themselves in the lobby’s curiosity cabinet, a revamped relic of the original building. Visitors are encouraged to sign the guestbook with a stamp of a dried leaf or flower.

The hotel offers just 44 accommodations — relatively large for a Mendocino property — including 14 double queen rooms, 25 king rooms and 5 junior suites. Within each room type, travelers can choose to upgrade to features such as a balcony or deck, an ocean view or both.

My room, a spacious King Junior Suite Ocean View, felt like a relaxing retreat with its muted color palette of greens, browns and yellows and its cozy linen spa robes. After a day of exploring Mendocino, I enjoyed relaxing on the sofa, perusing the coffee table book Botanicum, and sampling locally made goodies from the snack basket and minibar (for a fee).

Trailborn Hill House has one on-site restaurant: Pizza Standard Time, a casual bar and diner offering mostly pizza, plus salads, charcuterie boards and small Italian bites like arancini. The fare was limited but tasty; my friend and I tried a pizza, salad, and local Husch chardonnay and were quite happy. It’s nice having a quick, casual meal available on-site in case you arrive late and tired from the drive, but it’s also just a few minutes’ walk to Mendocino if you want more options.

Like all Trailborn properties, this one offers a lobby convenience store called Hill House Wine & Grocer. Guests can purchase local drinks and snacks (mostly the kind you’d find on a charcuterie board), plus apparel, toys, candles with the property’s signature scent and other souvenirs.

The hotel also offered a small but delicious complimentary breakfast spread. As with everything else during my stay, the breakfast was high-quality yet unpretentious, with guests serving and bussing their own tables. Instead of having a designated breakfast area, guests can find a cozy spot to eat inside Pizza Standard Time or the attached Cabot Cove Detective Library, outside by one of the fire pits or back to their room.

However, this will change when Trailborn’s second Mendocino property, The Mendocino Hotel, opens in 2027. Instead of complimentary breakfast, Hill House plans to provide guests with a voucher to Moonwave, The Mendocino Hotel’s dining concept, which will serve “coastal comfort” food three meals a day plus drinks at the lobby bar.

If you didn’t realize you were in a small town, you will as soon as you interact with any of the hotel staff — everyone I spoke to, from front desk staff to custodians, was beyond friendly.

As for amenities, they align with the brand’s laid-back, outdoorsy style and with some of the things the Mendocino area is known for. You’ll find:

Located just a few minutes’ walk (or bike ride) from downtown Mendocino, Hill House at Trailborn puts guests in the heart of the town’s charming boutiques and varied dining and drinking scene. But you won’t get bored if you hang around the property, either.

Here are some of the on-site activities guests may want to try:

While Mendocino’s remoteness makes it a haven for crowd-weary travelers, it’s becoming easier than ever to reach thanks to recent roadwork funding and new direct flights to Charles M. Schulz–Sonoma County Airport (STS), including on Alaska Airlines, Delta and Southwest. That’s one reason Mendo made TPG’s 2027 Where to Go list.

But travelers can also fly into San Francisco International Airport (SFO), Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK) or Sacramento International Airport (SAC), which are a bit farther away but offer more flight options.

Depending on the airport you choose, you’ll need to rent a car and drive two to four hours to Mendocino.

Basic rooms start as low as $140 per night in the off-season, while my King Junior Suite Ocean View starts around $350 per night (though these prices can climb much higher on summer weekends). Award rates start at 48,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night, or you could redeem a 50,000-point free night certificate.

When booking, you’ll want to use one of the credit cards that earn the most points for Marriott stays, as well as one that possibly offers automatic Marriott Bonvoy elite status for value-added benefits. These include:

The information for the Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Hill House has three wheelchair-accessible rooms, including two double queens and one king; these feature accessible tubs and, in some cases, roll-in showers. The property and its parking lot are also wheelchair accessible. For hearing-impaired guests, a portable kit can be installed in any room.

As a points traveler who loves Mendocino, I’m thrilled to see the town’s first points property not only opening but thriving. As a traveler who appreciates unique stays and has experienced some of the town’s charming independent properties, I’m also glad that Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino has brought enough character to fit seamlessly into the local scene.

It seems the Trailborn brand — and Marriott Bonvoy — is betting big on Mendocino. Hill House is one of two Mendocino properties purchased by The Trailborn brand. The second, the 150-year-old Mendocino Hotel, is undergoing renovation and slated to open in 2027.

#6151. FAA Projects Busiest Thanksgiving Travel Week in 16 Years

More than 417,000 flights will operate in the U.S. this week and early next week as Americans travel ahead of and after Thanksgiving, according to the FAA.

If accurate, that figure would translate to the busiest Thanksgiving travel period in 16 years.

Tuesday is expected to be the single busiest day of the interval, with more than 52,000 flights.

Air traffic will dip only slightly on Wednesday (49,831 flights) and nearly halve on Thanksgiving Day (27,619 flights) itself, the FAA said, with a rebound following Friday to Tuesday, Dec. 1. There will be over 50,000 flights per day on the Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday after Thanksgiving.

Perhaps aiming to assuage concerns from the public after a turbulent couple of weeks, transportation officials said they are prioritizing traveler safety and taking “unprecedented action” to limit flight delays and cancellations.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted that the Trump administration has assembled a “tiger team” of experts to prevent another mass ground stop.

“Our air traffic controllers and safety professionals are working around the clock to keep Americans moving during what is expected to be the busiest Thanksgiving travel week in 16 years,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement. “The growing demand for air travel makes it more important than ever to continue modernizing our air traffic control system and build a national airspace system for the 21st century.”

The FAA is also advising travelers to get to the airport early and check with their airline for updates if bad weather seems likely to impact their trip. The agency noted the high likelihood of thunderstorms in the Southeast, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast this week.

#6150. The Airbus A380 Burns Over 3,000 Gallons An Hour & Still Pays Off For Emirates

The Airbus A380 burns far more than 3,000 gallons (approximately 11,356 liters) of fuel every single hour, significantly higher than what would be expected from a modern widebody aircraft. Despite the high figure, Emirates keeps the four-engine superjumbo central to its long-haul network. Across the wider airline industry, most carriers have scaled back, parked, or retired their double-deckers because four engines bring steep fuel burn and heavy maintenance demands on ordinary routes. Emirates has defied this trend and continues to fly the aircraft across major global trunk routes, honing the high hourly consumption into a core element of its commercial strategy.

How can an airframe that consumes thousands of gallons per hour still pay off when other airlines view it as a commercial liability? Success ultimately comes from filling hundreds of seats on flights into slot-constrained airports backed by strong connecting hub traffic. Looking closely at the A380's fuel burn, per-seat economics, hub advantages, financial track record, and future outlook, it becomes clear that the type still makes sense for Emirates.

On an hourly basis, the A380's fuel consumption stands out immediately against modern twin-engine long-haul aircraft. Figures cited by Simple Flying place the A380's fuel burn at roughly 4,600 gallons (approximately 17,413 liters) per hour, nearly double the roughly 2,700 gallons (approximately 10,221 liters) per hour burned by an Airbus A350-1000. That wide gap stems from four large turbofans moving a heavier double-deck airframe across long sectors, where takeoff weight, cruise altitude, headwinds, and route length continually shape exact hourly consumption.

Emirates President Tim Clark has framed that hourly fuel burn in weight terms as well as volume, as noted by Airline Ratings. On a long-haul flight from Dubai International Airport (DXB) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) carrying 515 passengers, Clark has indicated that fuel burn runs around 13 tonnes (approximately 28,660 pounds) per hour. Across the full trip between the two hubs, total fuel burn reaches roughly 200 tonnes (approximately 440,925 pounds).

Those figures show why the A380 looks daunting whenever an airline evaluates raw fuel burn in isolation rather than total seat capacity. Burning that much fuel every hour creates a substantial fuel bill on paper, which will naturally lead most airlines to look elsewhere for widebody capacity. With that in mind, it seems somewhat nonsensical for Emirates to stick with the A380 when all its rivals have ceded to the extortionate costs.

Once fuel burn is divided across hundreds of seats, not just being viewed purely per hour, the A380's commercial math changes sharply. Using the Dubai-to-Los Angeles comparison noted by AirlineRatings, Emirates President Tim Clark has explained that the A380's fuel cost per seat can beat running two Boeing 787 flights, each of which burns roughly half as much fuel as the superjumbo. That advantage holds when high load factors keep cabins well filled, whereas flying a large double-decker with dozens of empty seats quickly destroys per-passenger efficiency.

Slot-constrained airports turn that high seat count into an even bigger practical asset on trunk routes. As The Economist reports, scarce runway and terminal slots at congested hubs such as London Heathrow (LHR) and Hong Kong (HKG) limit how often an airline can land or take off. Putting a 787 into a single Heathrow slot where a 517-seat A380 can operate leaves far fewer seats for sale at peak demand, not something that Emirates sees as acceptable.

Emirates reinforces those slot economics through its connecting hub in Dubai, which pulls transfer passengers from across continents onto high-capacity long-haul flights. Whereas other major airports focus on point-to-point local demand at either end of a route, Dubai funnels connecting traffic into large cabins, so seat occupancy stays consistently high. Together, scarce slots at major destinations and steady transfer flows at Dubai give Emirates the passenger volume needed to make high seat counts pay off.

The Airbus A380 can fly up to 16 hours nonstop. Here’s how its massive fuel capacity and range make ultra-long-haul flights possible.

Few other carriers share the exact combination of network scale, slot pressure, and hub geography that lets Emirates run the A380 so consistently. Reporting from Simple Flying highlights that Emirates built its entire long-haul model around funneling global connecting traffic through Dubai onto high-capacity trunk routes. Many other airlines rely more heavily on local point-to-point demand or spread flying across fragmented secondary markets, where filling 500 seats every day is much harder to do consistently.

Differences in hub structure and slot portfolios also explain why rival operators often reach different conclusions about the double-decker. While some airlines face tight runway caps at destinations, they may lack a central connecting hub with the same global reach or fleet concentration to keep large cabins full across seasons. When demand dips or seasonal swings hit, carrying hundreds of empty seats penalizes operating margins far more severely than operating smaller twin-aisle jets.

Those structural contrasts help explain why several carriers have parked or retired A380 aircraft earlier than Emirates, and why others have not made the A380 the focal point of their fleet. Take Air France, for example: the airline retired all its A380 aircraft in 2020, primarily because it could not fillseats like Emirates can. Without Emirates' specific mix of connecting scale and high-volume trunk demand, replicating its A380 formula remains out of reach for most airlines.

The A380's commercial case at Emirates is backed by years of financial results, not just theoretical seat math. Before the pandemic, Emirates President Tim Clark told Simple Flying that roughly 85% of Emirates' profits came from the A380 because the double-decker stayed consistently full and drew strong demand across every cabin. High occupancy across first, business, and economy turned those large passenger counts into substantial earnings across long-haul trunk routes.

That profit contribution has carried into Emirates' modern record run even as fuel expenses and operating costs remain closely watched. As detailed by Aviation Week and Emirates' 2025–26 annual financial results, Clark recently pointed to the A380 as the most profitable asset in Emirates' fleet during its record financial year. Broad demand for premium and main cabins helped support those results.

End-of-year financial figures highlight the scale of that record performance across both the airline and the wider group. Emirates' 2025–26 financial disclosures show Emirates Group reported a record profit of AED 24.4 billion (approximately $6.6 billion) for 2025–26, while Emirates airline posted a record profit before tax of AED 22.8 billion (approximately $6.2 billion). Together, those numbers show how well-filled A380 cabins can underpin strong financial returns and provide hard proof that the A380 remains a financially viable aircraft for Emirates.

Emirates operates many long-haul routes from its hub in Dubai with the huge A380, but which are the longest offered?

Looking ahead, Emirates plans to keep its A380 fleet flying until roughly 2041, giving the double-decker a long runway in service even after production ended in 2021. Coverage from Simple Flying and Executive Traveller notes that Emirates has worked to keep the fleet flying for years to come while weighing what comes next at the top end of its widebody lineup. Extending A380 operations toward 2041 reflects how central high-capacity flying remains to the airline's long-term fleet plan.

To keep that superjumbo presence going with modern efficiency, Emirates President Tim Clark has floated a modernized A380neo concept and signaled readiness to order at least 100 aircraft, according to reporting in Executive Traveller. Clark estimates a re-engined and updated A380neo could burn around nine tonnes (approximately 19,842 pounds) of fuel per hour, which would narrow the running-cost gap against newer twinjets. From Emirates' perspective, a 100-jet commitment means the A380 should ideally continue operating well beyond 2041, as long as Airbus can find a way to improve its economics.

Airbus, however, has set a much higher bar before reviving the program, reportedly pointing to roughly 250 orders needed to make a restart commercially viable. That gap between a 100-aircraft minimum order and a 250-order threshold creates a clear standoff with no launched A380neo program on the board. Unless order volume or manufacturing economics shift dramatically, Emirates' plan for 2041 rests on its existing fleet rather than a newly built A380neo.

The A380's story at Emirates shows why high hourly fuel burn does not automatically doom a large aircraft when operating conditions line up. Burning roughly 4,600 gallons (approximately 17,413 liters) of jet fuel per hour looks daunting on paper, but high passenger loads, lower per-seat fuel burn than twin-aisle alternatives on busy trunks, scarce slots at hubs, and steady connecting flows through Dubai allow Emirates to turn that capacity into strong financial returns.

The A380 is still more of a specialized tool, not something viable across the wider industry. Few airlines possess the hub geography, slot portfolio, and connecting traffic scale required to keep five hundred-plus seats consistently full across long-haul sectors year after year through seasonal peaks and troughs. For Emirates, however, high hourly fuel burn and high seating capacity are two sides of the same commercial equation as long as trunk demand and connecting flows stay strong.

#6149. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”

Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

“I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

“This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”

He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

“I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”

The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6146. Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”

Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”

“Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”

Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”

“We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

“I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”

Several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”

Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

“Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”

“The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

“I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

“They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

“We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”

“That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”

Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”

Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

“I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”

#6145. Norse Atlantic Says Financial Situation ‘Critical’

After close to a year of dire financial warnings, Norway’s Norse Atlantic Airways said Wednesday that its situation is “critical” and that it must obtain short-term financing to continue operations.

The Arendal-based carrier has struggled with higher jet fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. In the months since the war started, the airline has cut staff, furloughed some crew members, suspended unprofitable routes, and instituted temporary pay reductions for some non-flying crew, but these steps have apparently not put Norse Atlantic back on solid ground.

“[The company’s financial condition is] dependent on securing financing to meet its short term liquidity needs and to continue its operations,” officials said in a statement. “Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover.”

“Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution,” the message continued. “Norse will provide further information as and when appropriate.”

Rising fuel costs have set back airlines around the world, but the squeeze is arguably worst in Europe, since the continent depends mainly on Gulf oil and has little domestic refining capacity. The crisis has forced Latvia’s airBaltic into bankruptcy, teed up EasyJet’s sale to Apollo Global Management, and inflicted considerable damage on Lufthansa’s core brand.

It was not immediately clear if Norse Atlantic has any candidates in mind for a potential merger. The carrier is not part of any global airline alliance, though it partners with operators such as EasyJet, Norwegian Air Shuttle, and Pegasus through its Norse Connections program.

Bloomberg reported in 2023 and 2024 that the carrier was weighing alliances with larger airlines, possibly through an equity stake, but none were named.

Norse Atlantic operates only long-haul flights. Its network has been adjusted multiple times over the last year in an effort to reduce costs.

Star Alliance member Air New Zealand is gearing up to commence its newest long-haul service, as the airline adds Christchurch (CHC) to Perth (PER) from November 30. This will be the first time the airline has operated the city pair since it terminated the nonstop service from New Zealand's South Island in 2019.

The flights are set to run seasonally, three times a week, providing another alternative for travelers looking to experience Australia's West Coast. Air New Zealand will face competition on the route, as Jetstar also operates a seasonal service.

The airline's decision to resume services to Perth came in the same announcement ​​​​​ as the carrier added Singapore (SIN) and Tokyo Narita (NRT) from the Garden City. Christchurch is the second largest city in the South Pacific nation, and its airport is the only one in the South Island equipped for widebody aircraft.

Air New Zealand will resume the service to Perth on November 30, and operate the flight up to three times a week through until May 7. These flights will complement the airline's existing year-round service from Auckland (AKL).

These new flights will add up to an additional 37,000 seats across the Southern Hemisphere summer season, and are a welcome addition to the Southern airports expansion, off the back of a successful season of short-haul seasonal flights to Rarotonga (RAR). The flights to Perth will follow the schedule detailed in the table above.

The resumption of services to Perth from Christchurch will cater to strong travel demand that otherwise has seen travelers forced to connect via other airports, including Auckland, Brisbane, Melbourne or Sydney. As already mentioned, Jetstar, the low-cost subsidiary of the Qantas Group, commenced its own seasonal service from Perth to Christchurch with its Airbus A321LR narrowbody twinjets.

These services are expected to run through until late March. Air New Zealand's return to the city pair marks the only widebody and aircraft with premium cabins serving the route. Jetstar's schedule is detailed in the table below.

Air New Zealand has an extensive domestic and trans-Tasman network from Christchurch, and the new service will be popular with both leisure and business travelers. Those visiting the South Island can now transit via Christchurch Airport from other airports across the island, without the need to travel via another major hub.

Low-cost carrier Jetstar prepares to launch its first-ever flights between Western Australia and New Zealand's South Island.

With Air New Zealand having commenced its nonstop services from Christchurch to Singapore on October 28, this marked the airline's resumption of the route since it was suspended in February 2020. On the day of the first flight this year, the carrier announced that it would actually expand its schedule to year-round.

This complements the existing daily Singapore Airlines service to Christchurch, on which it partners through a joint venture. Services from Christchurch to Tokyo Narita also take flight on November 28, providing nonstop services to the Japanese capital through until late May. Air New Zealand previously operated nonstop flights between the two cities up until 2015.

While not operated with long-haul aircraft, Air New Zealand also quietly resumed nonstop services from Christchurch to Adelaide (ADL) in October. This route is served twice weekly onboard the carrier's Airbus A320 or A321neo, and will continue through to the end of March.

The Norway-based long-haul budget airline officially ceased operations and filed for bankruptcy on Friday after failing to raise the cash necessary to keep flying.

The bankruptcy filing comes two days after Pakistan International Airlines, which contracts Norse to operate select flights, said on X that Norse had suspended operations "without prior notice."

Norse flew just one U.S. route at the time of its shut down: Orlando International Airport (MCO) to London's Gatwick Airport (LGW), schedules from aviation analytics firm Cirium show.

During the prime summer months, Norse also seasonally flew from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Athens International Airport (ATH) in Greece, LGW and Rome's Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci International Airport (FCO).

At its peak in 2024, Norse served five U.S. destinations, including Las Vegas's Harry Reid International Airport (LAS), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Miami International Airport (MIA), from gateways in Europe.

The collapse of Norse comes at a challenging time for airlines. Jet fuel is at historic highs, spiking after Iran war and other conflicts. Geopolitical tensions have closed significant swaths of airspace, including Russia and significant portions of the Middle East. And, high interest rates have pushed the cost of capital for any business to the highest levels in years.

Norse warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical" and said its continued operation was "dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs."

Luis Gallego, the CEO of International Airlines Group that owns British Airways and Iberia, told the Financial Times in October that smaller airlines would struggle this winter due to the those financial headwinds.

Norse was one of the last airlines trying to make long-haul, low-cost work between the U.S. and Europe. Play Airlines, which attempted the same strategy via a connecting hub at Iceland's Keflavik International Airport (KEF), shut down in September 2025. And both Norse and Play were formed following the retrenchment and collapse of previous attempts; Norse from Norwegian Air's withdrawal from the market in 2021 and Play from the ashes of WOW Air that shut down in 2019.

Only independent French Bee and the budget arms of the larger European airline groups, including Discover, Level and Edelweiss Air, continue to offer lower-cost transatlantic flights.

Story updated with Norse confirmation of its shut down and subsequent bankruptcy filing.

#6142. Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)

Former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

"56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot."

In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

#6141. The New Airbus A220 Coming In 2027

The Airbus A220 is currently preparing for a major upgrade, although the manufacturer is falling short of launching a new variant altogether. This year, new Airbus A220 deliveries will be outfitted with the manufacturer's Airspace interior, aligning the A220 with the interior feel of the A350, A330neo, and A320neo. Highlights include new upgraded extra-large overhead lockers, which will be around 20% lighter while offering more than 15% additional baggage capacity.

These aircraft will also feature 16-million-color LED lighting, allowing airlines to tailor their brand or flight phases. Airbus also plans on offering this unique interior as a retrofit option for existing Airbus A220 customers. Meanwhile, starting in 2027, a higher-density Airbus A220-300, one that features a 160-seat layout, will be offered, which provides operators with additional revenue and unit-cost gains without introducing a larger model to any given route.

However, the much-discussed Airbus A220-500 variant remains unannounced, and it does not look like Airbus has any plans to make any quick moves there as well. The manufacturer has looked to continue improving the profitability of the Airbus A220 family while also improving production rates, offering even more flexibility for operators. Let's analyze all the upcoming changes to the Airbus A220 family.

To contextualize the upcoming upgrades to this extremely popular aircraft program, it is important to begin by breaking down the Airbus A220's origins and discussing the aircraft's industrial footprint. The Airbus A220 began its life as a member of the Bombardier CSeries, a five-abreast narrowbody jet which was launched on July 13, 2008, with the intent of bridging the gap between regional jets and larger single-aisle aircraft.

It was first introduced to the market as the CS100, and it first took to the skies on September 16, 2013, before being certified by Transport Canada on December 18, 2015. The jet entered service with SWISS on July 15, 2016. The Bombardier CS300, which flew on February 27, 2015, would be certified on July 11, 2016, and it entered service on December 14 of that year with launch customer airBaltic.\

In July 2018, after Airbus took a majority stake in the company, it was quickly rebranded as the Airbus A220 and later organized as Airbus Canada Limited Partnership in June 2019. The aircraft program was now fully in the hands of manufacturing giant Airbus. The manufacturer's industrial capacity was expanded beyond Mirabel, Quebec, with a second final assembly line opened in Mobile, Alabama, in August 2019.

This allowed the manufacturer to avoid hefty import duties from US regulators. The manufacturer's ownership stake was increased to 75% in February 2020, with Bombardier electing to exit the program. The Airbus A220 remains the only commercial program managed by the manufacturer entirely outside of Europe. After entering service, the aircraft quickly established itself as offering strong dispatch reliability and improved passenger satisfaction over other models.

The Airbus A220 is powered by Pratt & Whitney PW1500G geared turbofan engines, and the aircraft offers a carbon-composite lightweight wing and an aluminum-lithium fuselage. Fly-by-wire controls and refined aerodynamics help deliver long legs and low-cost operations. Family weights range from 63 to 71 tonnes (139,000-156,000 lbs) of maximum takeoff weight (MTOW).

The aircraft family offers a range of 6,390-6,670 km (3,450-3,600 nautical miles), making it capable of serving almost all transcontinental niches in the United States and even longer-range lower-gauge routes within Europe. The 35 m (115 ft) Airbus A220-100 seats around 108-133 passengers, while the longer A220-300 seats a larger 130-160 passengers, depending on the specific configuration.

Airbus also launched the ACJ TwoTwenty business-jet variant, which was launched in late 2020. Delta remains the largest customer for the aircraft, and, globally, more than 1,100 Airbus A220s have been ordered, with over 500 delivered to date.

Globally, the fleet has surpassed 1.5 million flights and 2.7 million block hours, with the aircraft carrying more than 100 million passengers. The aircraft has also managed to maintain an exceptional safety reputation, with only one non-fatal smoke-related accident showing up on its rap sheet. It mainly competes with the Embraer E-Jet E2 family, holding a 55% share in this small-airliner niche, demonstrating the success and competitive value this program offers.

Airbus already operates several variants in its A220 series.

The A220 has slowly matured from being a promising upstart in the industry to becoming a core single-aisle workhorse for most carriers, especially with airlines wanting more revenue, lower unit costs, and a cabin that matches the rest of the manufacturer's portfolio. The five-abreast Airbus A220 already offers exceptional passenger comfort and impressive fuel burn, but bin space, lighting, and brand cohesion lag behind the newest Airbus models. Bringing the Airspace cabin to the aircraft helps close this gap.

Airlines today are extremely focused on premium and brand perception, and improving interiors is a key element of this overall strategy. From a commercial perspective, airlines need a low-risk way to add seats without adding a new aircraft type. The 160-seat Airbus A220-300 adds about ten more seats while providing more attractive costs per available seat mile, which ultimately proved useful for capacity-constrained layouts where upgauging to an A320neo would negatively impact profitability.

From a strategic perspective, Airbus needs to widen the A220's overall addressable market and strengthen the plane's business case before choosing to green-light a stretch to the Airbus A220-500. After all, the manufacturer wants to continue improving cabin appeal for legacy operators first.

Throughout this retrofitting and upgrade process, Airbus is mainly looking to pull two key levers. This year, new Airbus A220 deliveries will adopt the new Airbus Airspace cabin, a similar design that has been seen on Airbus A350, Airbus A330neo, and Airbus A320neo jets. Headlines are quick to discuss the 16-million-color LED lighting, which brand-matches the ambiance and circadian cues across different flight phases.

However, the Airspace kit also standardizes modern trim, surfaces, and touchpoints so that the aircraft will resemble any other Airbus model as closely as possible. Airbus is also quick to point out that it will be offering flexibility to operators, specifically when it comes to high-density Airbus A220-300 models. This ensures that its upgrades are not only providing optionality to future customers, but also letting existing operators improve their fleets.

The idea of stretching to the Airbus A220-500 also brings a lot to the table, as this model would upgauge the family and could potentially fill a capacity gap (albeit a small one) that exists in the Airbus commercial lineup. These upgrades are an extremely low-risk way to improve its product offering quickly.

Do Airbus or Embraer's narrow-bodied airlines dominate the short-haul and regional market?

From a financial perspective, the A220 upgrades represent a relatively low-risk lever being pulled by Airbus. For operators, these upgraded cabins will lift premium appeal, especially when it comes to corporate travelers who are interested in flying more modern aircraft. This will also result in more loyalty captured across the board.

Larger overhead bins are beneficial for operators, as they enable them to have lower gate-check-related costs and faster aircraft turns. Higher-capacity A220 variants can lower unit costs by spreading overall expenses out over more seats and adding capacity at slot-constrained airports and during peak leisure travel seasons.

Investing in these upgrades comes with low risks as aircraft downtimes are relatively low. This refresh supports overall pricing and will hopefully accelerate Airbus' order momentum: Delta, for example, is in the process of replacing its aging Boeing 717 fleet with advanced Airbus A220 models. This will improve learning-curve economics all along the way, ultimately pushing the program toward profitability before the A220-500 stretch.

Airbus is investing in the A220 to make it even more competitive. Here's what's new and what's coming in the future for the smallest Airbus.

At the end of the day, all of this means relatively little for passengers. The upgraded A220 cabins will likely provide a marginally more comfortable passenger experience, thanks to the cabin lighting being a little nicer, and it is also less likely with these new cabins that passengers will have to place their bags far away from where they currently are.

In the grand scheme of things, these are very marginal changes likely to have a small impact on your experience as a traveler. On the other hand, the higher-capacity variants of the aircraft will likely result in less available room per passenger, reducing comfort across the board. It will certainly be interesting to see if the high-capacity variant coming in 2027 will pave the way for a stretched A220-500.

#6138. China Southern Orders 50 737 MAX Jets

A subsidiary of China Southern Airlines has agreed to buy 50 Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft, Reuters reported Tuesday.

The airplanes, which have a total list price of $7.4 billion, will be used by Xiamen Airlines, which is based in Fujian. Deliveries are expected from 2031 to 2034.

The deal is Boeing’s largest with a Chinese operator in nearly a decade. The country largely shifted toward Airbus aircraft as relations with the U.S. frayed.

President Donald Trump hoped to reverse that trend during his state visit to China in May. Trump discussed a potential purchase directly with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and even brought along Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg for the summit. Ultimately, Beijing agreed to buy 200 aircraft from Boeing, fewer than analysts expected, but still notable considering Boeing’s drought in the country.

Trump said earlier this week that he thinks China will buy 250 more aircraft from Boeing. He did not provide details or say where that information came from.

China Southern said the new aircraft will help Xiamen expand after it relocates to the new Xiamen Xiang’an International Airport. The facility will replace Xiamen Gaoqi International Airport as Xiamen’s main gateway.
