#6136. 5 Mid-Sized US Airport Projects Quietly Adding Gates & Merging Security Checkpoints In 2026

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

Billion-dollar terminal programs at Chicago, Los Angeles, and New York tend to dominate airport construction headlines, but some of the most practical upgrades in the country are happening one tier down. Medium-sized airports that grew quickly over the last decade are now dealing with the same problem: too few gates for the flights airlines want to add, and terminals split into separate wings that each need their own security checkpoint. For passengers, that layout often means picking the right checkpoint before knowing which gate is free, and for airlines, it limits where new service can go.

The five projects below take different routes to the same goal. Some add gates, others knock down the walls between concourses so a single checkpoint can feed every gate, and a few do both. Each has also hit a visible milestone in 2026, whether that is new gates opening to passengers, a finished concourse, a design contract, or steel rising on a replacement terminal, even though most of the work will not wrap up until 2028 or 2029.

Eppley Airfield (OMA) in Omaha is the furthest along of the projects on this list. In November 2026, passengers got their first look at the $950 million Build OMA Terminal Modernization Program, which the Omaha Airport Authority approved to nearly double the terminal's size. According to Travel Weekly, the building will grow from 375,000 square feet (34,839 square meters) to 646,000 square feet (60,015 square meters), and the expansion adds two gates for international flights along with a customs hall. Holder Construction is managing the work, which broke ground in February 2024 on a terminal that had not been modernized since the 1980s.

Four new gates, numbered A1, A1A, A1B and A2, opened on November 4, 2026. Airways Magazine reported that Delta Air Lines was using the new space in place of its previous south concourse gates, with passengers reaching the area through the existing south terminal and its current checkpoint, an arrangement that will only last until the rest of the building opens. Once finished, the unified concourse will connect the terminal areas that are separated today, and every departing passenger will clear a centralized TSA checkpoint in a new central pavilion that also houses a food court and shops.

The timeline beyond that is already set. Airways reports that the central pavilion and more of the concourse should open in early 2027, followed by new baggage and ticketing systems in mid-2027, and WOWT reported that the full program remains on time and on budget for completion in 2028. Steady demand is driving the work. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) data shows Eppley enplaned 2,565,135 passengers in 2025, a 0.70% dip from the prior year, but the airport still set a monthly record of 530,157 passengers in June 2026, according to WOWT. Construction stood at 60% complete in September 2026.

Spokane International Airport (GEG) technically sits in the FAA’s small hub category, with 2,106,307 enplanements in 2025, but it is the second-busiest airport in Washington and runs a terminal program on a medium-hub scale. Its Terminal Renovation and Expansion program, known as TREX, began with a $150 million expansion of Concourse C. The first part, Concourse C West, opened in May 2024 with three new gates and six new ticket counters. The second part, Concourse C East, replaced ground boarding with three new passenger boarding bridges at gates C1 through C3, and the airport announced the full Concourse C project complete on May 26, 2026.

That finished concourse sets up the larger second phase. Today, Spokane operates two siloed terminals, so passengers screen separately for the A and B concourses or for Concourse C. The new Central Hall will consolidate security screening for all airlines into one checkpoint and add a post-security hall connecting all three concourses. As the Spokesman-Review reports, the building will place baggage claim on the ground floor and security screening on the second. Utility relocation along the front curb began in May 2026 to clear the site.

The scope has grown considerably since planning began, both in floor area and in cost. A January 2023 filing with Washington’s Department of Enterprise Services described a 145,000-square-foot (13,471 square meters) Central Hall with an estimated maximum price of $152 million. The Journal of Business now puts the project at 255,000 square feet (23,690 square meters) and an estimated $335 million. Simple Flying has detailed how the hall will end repeat screening by 2030. Growth explains the larger footprint, since by then the airport expects roughly 6.2 million annual passengers, according to the Daily Journal of Commerce.

Gone are the days when only the largest airports got the big money improvements. Here are six regional airports that are investing billions.

The largest project here belongs to John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH). The CMH Next program is a roughly $2 billion replacement terminal, and WHIO noted it is the most expensive public works project ever undertaken in Franklin County. Columbus also leads this group in traffic by a wide margin, with 4,396,625 enplanements in 2025 according to the FAA, and the Columbus Regional Airport Authority reported nearly 9.4 million passengers across its airports that year. The existing terminal opened in 1958 and will be demolished once the new building is ready.

Unlike Omaha and Spokane, Columbus is not stitching older buildings together. Spectrum News reported that the approved plan includes a 36-gate terminal and a central marketplace with just one security checkpoint, replacing the three checkpoints the airport operates today. According to Construction Equipment Guide, those 36 gates are seven more than CMH currently uses, and two will handle international flights with on-site customs facilities. Gensler designed the building, which comes in at just over 1 million square feet (92,903 square meters) and adds 40% to 60% more waiting area at the gates, according to Archinect.

Progress in 2026 is mostly structural, with crews now working vertically on the terminal itself. Construction began in December 2024, focused first on a new elevated roadway, and the first steel beam for the building went up on August 8, 2025. Construction Equipment Guide reported in October 2026 that the authority now expects completion in January 2029. That date is deliberate, since Axios notes that the opening is timed to coincide with the airport’s 100th anniversary. Once the move happens, the old terminal site will become additional overnight parking for aircraft, letting airlines position more planes for early morning departures.

Richmond International Airport (RIC) is the newest medium hub on this list. The airport was classified as a small hub based on 2024 data, but FAA figures for 2025 list it as a medium hub after it enplaned 2,481,863 passengers, a 1.04% increase. That growth has put pressure on a terminal where passengers heading to the A and B concourses use two separate TSA checkpoints. The Capital Region Airport Commission, which runs the airport, describes the planned Consolidated Security Screening Checkpoint as among the most transformative projects in RIC’s history.

According to AviationPros, the project is estimated at about $253.1 million. It includes about 103,000 square feet (9,569 square meters) of new construction, renovation of 84,000 square feet (7,804 square meters) of existing space on the first and second floors, and roughly 29,000 square feet (2,694 square meters) of mezzanine. Richmond BizSense reports that the merged checkpoint will open with 10 screening lanes, with room to expand to 14, and that the work will also reshape the main atrium and add space for concessions beyond security.

The 2026 milestones at Richmond have focused on securing funding and finalizing the design. In May, the FAA awarded Richmond a $5.8 million grant toward construction, and Senator Mark Warner’s office noted that the rest will come from a mix of federal, state, airport and passenger facility charge revenue, along with bonds. On October 27, the commission approved design contracts that put a team led by architecture firm Gresham Smith officially in charge of the checkpoint, according to Richmond BizSense. Airport officials plan to build in phases to limit disruption, though travelers may see checkpoint locations shift during construction. A firm opening date has not yet been published.

Spokane Airport is investing millions in a new Central Hall to connect three concourses, consolidate security, and eliminate repeat screening by 2030.

Boise Airport (BOI) is the outlier on this list because its project focuses on gates rather than checkpoints. Traffic has quickly outgrown the current terminal. According to Engineering News-Record, passenger traffic has climbed 81% over the past decade, and FAA data shows 2,579,647 enplanements in 2025, up 4.21% from 2024. Boise was reclassified from a small hub to a medium hub after that growth, which added federal requirements for passenger services and airline competition plans. The airport also shares its airfield with the Idaho Air National Guard at Gowen Field.

In August 2025, the Boise City Council approved Hensel Phelps as construction manager and general contractor for the Concourse A and Terminal Improvements project. The city states that the contract carries a not-to-exceed amount of $700 million for work scheduled through 2029. Its centerpiece is Concourse A, which will add up to 10 new gates for future air service. The package also covers an expanded back-of-house baggage handling system, a new central utility plant, and two phases of improvements to passenger flow inside the existing terminal.

No local tax money is involved. KIVI reported that the project will be paid for with airport revenue and passenger facility charges, not local tax dollars. The broader BOI Upgrade program began in 2019, but the project stalled during the pandemic and was later redesigned to handle more passengers. Concourse A remains in design with Fentress Architects and Jacobs, and the airport states that construction is set to begin in 2026. Boise does not plan a checkpoint merger as part of this contract, so its case shows that some mid-sized airports need more gates first, while others need to simplify how passengers reach the gates they already have.

#6135. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

Colombian flag carrier Avianca is adding a new connection to the U.S. Northeast.

#6132. The Airbus A350’s Unique Cabin Design That Sets It Apart From Others

The Airbus A350 has silently become one of the most recognizable long-haul aircraft in the skies today, but its most distinctive asset is likely not going to be its curved wingtips or ultra-efficient engines, but rather the aircraft's cabin itself. From the beginning, Airbus designed the A350's cross-section and interior architecture around overall passenger wellbeing, before wrapping that in the airline's 'Airspace' design language.

The aircraft features higher ceilings, wider sidewalls, and large overhead bins that all combine with low cabin noise, large windows, and advanced air management systems in order to create a noticeably calmer environment on long flights. Humidity and overall cabin pressure levels remain optimized to reduce jet lag and fatigue, while carefully engineered lighting schemes help allow passengers to adjust to new time zones.

Airlines, on the other hand, get a flexible interior shell that they can tune for all kinds of routes. As more carriers introduce refreshed Airbus A350 interiors and Airbus rolls out its New Production Standard with wider, longer cabins, the aircraft is increasingly beginning to set a benchmark for how a modern long-haul cabin should feel.

It also showcases why cabin design matters just as much as range or fuel burn for passengers and airlines alike. For many travellers, the first step onto an Airbus A350 instantly signals a different kind of widebody experience for passengers that an airline can market.

Originally launched as the Airbus XWB (which stands for 'eXtra-Wide-Body'), the A350 family was developed as a clean-sheet, long-range twin-engine aircraft designed to replace earlier four-engine types and to compete directly with the Boeing 787 and 777. Originally built from carbon-fibre reinforced plastic, the aircraft combines a lightweight fuselage with a high-aspect-ratio wing and Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines.

These turbofans deliver double-digit fuel-burn and carbon emissions reductions over older widebodies. The family today spans the Airbus A350-900, the ultra-long-range Airbus A350-900ULR, and the stretched Airbus A350-1000, in addition to the forthcoming Airbus A350F freighter, giving airlines a common cockpit and systems across multiple mission profiles.

Typical three-class layouts seat roughly 300 to 380 passengers, with range figures comfortably exceeding 8,000 miles (12,875 km) on passenger variants. Airbus has continued to refine the platform using its New Production Standard, trimming weight across the board, and significantly improving take-off performance while unlocking extra usable cabin length and width.

The table above details some additional specifications for the Airbus A350, according to documents published by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency. Orders have now passed 1,600, with hundreds already in service and a growing backlog from both established network carriers and fast-growing new market entrants.

Operational data now shows that the global Airbus A350 fleet has flown well over a million sectors on more than a thousand routes, with an excellent safety record and strong overall dispatch reliability. For airlines, that translates into the ability to open thinner long-haul city pairs while upgauging older fleets on trunk routes and standardizing on a single modern widebody family.

What differentiates the Airbus A350 most from its rivals is its Airspace cabin architecture. The fuselage cross-section was shaped to maximize usable interior width between the sidewalls, giving designers more shoulder room at seated eye level than earlier Airbus types and many competing jet models.

That extra space can thus be spent on wider seats, broader aisles, larger armrests, or a mix of all three, depending on each airline's philosophy. An improved cabin experience offers a lot of comfort and versatility for passengers, allowing airlines to charge more for these kinds of premium seats.

High ceilings, carefully sculpted sidewalls, and large pivoting overhead bins create a sense of openness while still giving generous space for passengers to easily stow carry-on bags. The cabin is also engineered for comfort on a microscopic level, with higher humidity, lower effective cabin altitude, and very low noise levels that all help reduce fatigue on long-haul overnight sectors.

With the latest New Production Standard, Airbus has subtly widened and stretched the cabin envelope. This has freed up space for larger galleys, new crew-rest arrangements, and ultimately additional seating options without the requirement to fundamentally change the feel of the aircraft's interior.

Combined with flexible lighting, advanced connectivity, and a step-by-step modification approach, the Airbus A350 offers airlines an unusually adaptable canvas for everything from minimalist economy layouts to highly differentiated four-class flagship aircraft.

Discover why the Airbus A350 offers the ultimate passenger experience — quieter cabins, roomier seats, and comfort praised by flyers worldwide.

The Airbus A350's geometry and flight control systems make it an unusually strong platform for offering premium cabin service. The aircraft's wide, oval-shaped cross-section supports spacious 1-2-1 business-class layouts that offer long beds and large side consoles that do not feel squeezed, all while leaving room for generous aisles and direct aisle access at every seat.

Lower overall cabin noise, advanced filtration, and higher humidity, all alongside a lower effective cabin altitude, all enhance sleep quality and overall well-being. This aligns nicely with what high-yield passengers are looking to get out of overnight flights. The New Production Standard adds roughly four inches of extra usable cabin width.

SWISS is another airline that will use the aircraft to introduce new kinds of premium cabins, with the carrier debuting its new SWISS Senses four-class concept, which includes enclosed first-class suites and door-equipped business-class seats. These projects highlight how the Airbus A350 gives designers the room and range to build truly differentiated flagship products, turning the cabin into a competitive weapon on the world's longest and most lucrative routes.

The Airbus A350 is not a niche experiment but rather a core long-haul workhorse for dozens of major airlines. By the summer of 2026, around 730 Airbus A350s were in service worldwide with roughly 40 different operators. The largest fleets sit with Singapore Airlines, Qatar Airways, Cathay Pacific, Air France, and Delta, all of which use the type as a long-haul flagship on key intercontinental routes.

Airlines in China, including Air China and Sichuan Airlines, deploy the A350 on domestic trunk routes as well as for long-haul services to Europe and North America. This allows them to capitalize on the aircraft's exceptional versatility and efficiency. In Europe, carriers such as Lufthansa, Iberia, Finnair, SAS, and Turkish Airlines use the Airbus A350 to modernize aging Airbus A340 and Airbus A330 fleets.

In the Middle East and Africa, Qatar Airways and Ethiopian Airlines have embraced the type for global hub-and-spoke operations. Newer long-haul brands like STARLUX in Taiwan and upcoming operators such as IndiGo and Riyadh Air are also turning to the Airbus A350, underscoring its appeal from full-service legacies to ambitious challengers.

Freighter and corporate variants are joining the mix as well, with cargo specialists and VIP customers ordering the Airbus A350F and the private ACJ350 respectively. This will extend the family's presence beyond traditional passenger airlines into high-yield logistics spaces and ultra-long-range private or government operations.

The future of the Airbus A350 looks increasingly central to long-haul aviation. Airbus has logged more than 1,400 orders for the type across both passenger and freighter variants, with several hundred aircraft still to be delivered to both established and new kinds of carriers. In the coming years, airlines like IndiGo, Riyadh Air, and Qantas are set to introduce large Airbus A350 fleets, using the model to open new long-haul markets and replace older twin- and quad-engine aircraft.

Emirates is also rolling out its brand-new Airbus A350 models on a handful of routes. At the same time, a first wave of cabin retrofits for older models is already well underway, with early customers looking to densify layouts, shift space towards premium cabins, supporting Airbus' dedicated A350 upgrade services, and third-party retrofit programs.

The arrival of the Airbus A350F will pull the manufacturer deeper into the cargo market, all while ultra-long-range projects like Qantas' Project Sunrise show how far the platform can be stretched. New premium concepts such as the SWISS Senses, which debuted on the Airbus A350-900 before spreading to other aircraft types, reinforce the aircraft's role as a launchpad for next-generation cabins.

As environmental pressure continues to intensify, the aircraft's combination of composite structure, efficient engines, and SAF-ready systems positions the Airbus A350 as a key tool for airlines pursuing lower-carbon long-haul networks. They will be able to do so without sacrificing passenger appeal.

Taken together, the Airbus A350 is as much a story of cabin innovation as it is of engineering. Airbus gave airlines a wide canvas, which they wrapped in the branding and marketing of the company's Airspace concept. This interior offers extra space, low noise, and generous natural lighting. The manufacturer also refined this design with the New Production Standard and other retrofit options.

Airlines use the aircraft as a flexible canvas for everything from dense leisure layouts to ultra-luxurious ultra-long-haul flagships. Guests gain quieter rides, better air quality, larger bins, and comfortable seating, especially when it comes to the premium cabins. For airlines, strong economics and a future-proof cabin make the Airbus A350 a standout choice for next-generation long-haul fleets for years to come.

It's that time of year again: Your last chance to plan your final flights or mattress runs of 2026 in order to snag last-minute elite status for next year.

If you hold Marriott Bonvoy elite status and aren't going to requalify for your status tier this year, there's good news: The program is extending its “soft landing” policy into 2027. With this policy, if you fail to requalify for your current status this year, you will only drop one tier from March 2027 until February 2028.

Related: Marriott elite status: What it is and how to earn it

Based on the program's elite-status policies, the Marriott Bonvoy status you earned in 2025 will expire at the end of February 2027 unless you requalify for your current level or higher in 2026. But what if you don't meet the threshold for the same or higher status?

That's where Marriott's generous soft landing policy comes in. Whether you qualify for a level far below your current status or don't qualify for status at all in 2026, you'll only drop one status tier in 2027.

According to Marriott's website, members who don't requalify for status will see their new, lower tier take effect in early March 2027, and they can enjoy this status through February 2028. Meanwhile, if you requalify for your existing tier or a higher tier, you will also hold this status through February 2028.

This soft landing policy, which Marriott has offered for years, is a win-win: It provides valuable benefits to elite members who weren't able to requalify for status, while giving them a reason to stay loyal to Marriott and perhaps try again for status next year.

Related: The complete guide to earning Marriott elite status with credit cards

Marriott Bonvoy elite status offers some excellent perks, such as room upgrades, late checkout and even lounge access. Thankfully, with this soft landing policy, mid- and upper-tier elite members who don’t requalify this year won’t be left empty-handed. You can still enjoy the benefits of the next-lower tier from March 2027 to February 2028.

For example, with Titanium Elite status, expiring Ambassador Elite members will enjoy many of the same perks of their current status, including complimentary breakfast at most brands, suite upgrades at check-in, 75% bonus points earned on stays and a status match to United MileagePlus Premier Silver status.

You should see your new Marriott status and updated expiration in early March.

#6130. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

#6128. Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

“As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”

Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., said part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

“They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

“I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said Monday. “I think he's backing down.”

Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a big reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”

“I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”

During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

“Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat said, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

“Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”

But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”

Trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the company’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”

Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”

“Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear issues dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”

#6127. ICAO Hosts Air Transport Conference, Elects New Council Members

Last week, ICAO headquarters in Montréal hosted the Seventh Worldwide Air Transport Conference, where member states and industry stakeholders gathered to set global policy priorities on aviation economic regulation, infrastructure financing, resilience, consumer protection, and sustainable growth.

Over 1,500 delegates from 154 member states and organizations attended the week-long event 13 years after the Sixth Conference in 2013. They discussed high-level topics in commercial aviation: modernizing economic and legal frameworks, investing in infrastructure and skilled workforces, and ensuring that innovation keeps pace with rapidly changing technologies and global demands.

“Broad agreement was reached on the need for harmonized, risk-based, and proportionate economic regulation that facilitates the adoption of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, automation, sustainable aviation fuels, and advanced air mobility solutions,” ICAO said in a press release during the conference.

Participants agreed on the value of frameworks that support innovation and investment for economic development. They stressed this especially for smaller landlocked states, which depend heavily on air connectivity for growth.

The conference supported modernizing air navigation infrastructure in line with ICAO’s Global Air Navigation Plan. It also supported liberalizing air service agreements without making liberalization conditional on infrastructure development, since new air links fostered by more liberal agreements are seen as key to economic growth.

However, all initiatives should be flexible enough to address local circumstances and should not burden developing states. ICAO’s statement continued: “The conference also reaffirmed that international standards are key to building effective, market-enabling policies and avoiding fragmentation that could impede cross-border air services. Delegates pointed to ICAO’s Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) as a successful example of this approach.”

Participants were asked to express their views on consumer protection legislation that has become an integral part of the legal framework for all air operators.

At the Sixth Worldwide Air Transport Conference in March 2013, ICAO was asked to develop core principles on consumer protection. The final document, adopted by the ICAO Council in 2015, contains provisions on:

The report for the Seventh Conference invites states to modernize their consumer protection frameworks, keeping them evidence-based, proportionate, accessible, and responsive to the changing realities of commercial air transport. It also says legislation should establish clear responsibilities for carriers, intermediaries, and other providers regarding information, complaints, and disruption assistance.

ICAO is expected to review its core principles while preserving national and regional flexibility. It is also expected to assess whether existing policies adequately cover online intermediaries and other overlooked situations.

Many member states cautioned against the ICAO Air Passenger Handbook proposed by IATA, because producing and maintaining a single repository covering many different national laws would be too costly.

The conference asked ICAO to “examine the need for harmonized, risk-based guidance on the use of AI in aviation, including common terminology and meaningful human oversight.”

The rapid development of AI and its unknown effects on aviation operations is a topic member states will need to monitor. ICAO will coordinate and facilitate international exchange, while states will oversee implementation to ensure that the technologies adopted are secure, interoperable, and consistent with cybersecurity and data-protection objectives.

ICAO will handle AI within its existing structure, as the proposal to create an ad hoc unit was not supported.

During the final two days of the conference, ICAO held an extraordinary session of its assembly to elect the four additional council members required by the entry into force of the 2013 protocol amending the Convention on International Civil Aviation. The council is the organization’s permanent governing body, accountable to the assembly and responsible for setting priorities and implementing its directions. Its membership increased from 36 to 40, and there are no permanent seats.

Six candidates competed for the four new seats: Ethiopia, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Oman, Thailand, and Turkey. In the vote on the final day, Kazakhstan and Thailand were not elected, and the other four states won seats.

The council now comprises Angola, Argentina, Australia, Belize, Brazil, Canada, China, Colombia, Cuba, Denmark, Ecuador, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Ethiopia, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Malaysia, Mali, Mexico, Morocco, Nigeria, Oman, Poland, Qatar, the Republic of Korea, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Turkey, Uganda, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, the U.S., and Uruguay.

The next elections will take place at the General Assembly in September 2028.

#6126. Two American Airlines 737s Collide On Taxiway At Reagan National, One Loses Winglet

Two American Airlines Boeing 737-800s collided while lining up on a taxiway at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) on Friday evening, with images of the aftermath showing one jet had its winglet torn off. Moments after the collision, a pilot told air traffic control (ATC) that the aircraft had moved "slightly over the hold short line" and had "swapped paint" with the American jet next to it.

The mishap occurred at around 5:10 PM local time near Runway 19 and involved American Flight 638 to Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) and American Flight 2152 to Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD). It is the second time in less than 20 months that two American-branded aircraft have collided while waiting to depart from DCA, following a similar wingtip collision in April 2025.

Flight tracking data shows that both 737s had taxied out and were lining up waiting to enter Runway 19, with Flight 2152 lined up behind Flight 638. When the controller instructed Flight 638 to hold short of the runway, one of its pilots reported that they had collided with a fellow American 737, before stating that they were unsure whether the two aircraft were still attached.

A pilot onboard Flight 2152 then confirmed, "Oh yeah, we got clipped," before stating that the two 737s had separated. Debris was then reported, with a pilot stating that a "whole winglet" had been torn off and was on the ground. Airport operations subsequently recovered the winglet, and both aircraft taxied back to their gates for inspection. An inbound Envoy Air aircraft was also ordered by ATC to go-around immediately after the incident.

In a statement to Simple Flying, American said that "the wingtips of both Boeing 737-800s made contact," and that both planes had been taken out of service for maintenance inspections. The airline added that passengers on both flights would depart later on Friday evening. Tracking data shows that Flight 2152 left at around 11:00 PM, while Flight 638 departed at 11:20 PM, representing a delay of around six hours for both flights. An American spokesperson said,

"While taxiing for departure at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA), an American Airlines aircraft made contact with another American aircraft."

Hold short lines consist of four yellow lines painted across a taxiway before it meets a runway, and are there to prevent potentially dangerous runway incursions. Two solid lines are on the taxiway side, while two dashed lines are on the runway side. Pilots must stop before the solid lines unless ATC has cleared them to enter the runway.

The taxiway leading to DCA's Runway 19 is wide enough to accommodate two aircraft lined up side-by-side, an arrangement attempted by both jets on Friday. The 737-800 has a wingspan of 117 feet 5 inches (35.8 meters) including winglets, and pilots are expected to maintain situational awareness to ensure sufficient clearance from other aircraft.

The Federal Aviation Administration has confirmed it is investigating the incident, while the extent of the damage will determine whether the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) also becomes involved. Under the NTSB's definitions, an incident without serious injuries is only classified as an accident if an aircraft sustains "substantial damage." Notably, this category specifically excludes damage to wingtips.

Winglets can really cut fuel consumption and costs, but engineers have to carefully weigh down sides.

Friday's incident is the latest in a series of ground collisions at major US airports in recent weeks. On November 14, a UPS Airlines Boeing 767 freighter and a Copa Airlines Boeing 737-800 collided at Miami International Airport (MIA) after the cargo jet taxied past the point where it had been instructed to give way.

On October 6, a Delta Air Lines Airbus A350 clipped the horizontal stabilizer of an Air Canada Boeing 777 being towed at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), leaving its winglet lodged in the 777's tail. Friday's collision also has similarities to an incident at DCA in April 2025, when two American Eagle regional jets clipped wings while waiting to depart, one of which had several members of Congress on board.

#6124. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

“Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”

“Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”

Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

“The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

“While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

“I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”

“I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

Wyndham Rewards recently revised its fixed award chart, expanding from three to four redemption tiers.

The 15,000- and 30,000-point tiers remain, while free nights now start at 5,000 points instead of 7,500. Wyndham also added a 45,000-point tier for a select number of its highest-tier hotels and redistributed thousands of properties across all four tiers.

The new top tier is 50% higher than the former 30,000-point maximum, a devaluation in anyone's book. However, the new astonishingly low 5,000-point tier was what caught my attention. What exactly do you get for so few Wyndham Rewards points?

As someone who can't resist a great deal, I checked into one of these hotels to find out whether it was an amazing new sweet spot or a night I would rather forget.

Related: Wyndham Rewards guide: How to earn and redeem points, elite status and more

On a recent visit to Kansas and Missouri, I checked the Wyndham Rewards website and saw that the area had several properties for just 5,000 points per night.

I chose the Super 8 by Wyndham Riverside/Kansas City, mainly for its proximity to the beautiful new Kansas City International Airport (MCI). The next morning, I was flying to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) before continuing to Europe in a lie-flat seat for less than the price of a cup of coffee.

At the time of booking, the hotel had a 2.8-out-of-5 score based on 84 ratings on Wyndham's website, which did not fill me with confidence. However, the Wyndham Rewards member rate for my night was $96.21 including taxes and fees. Redeeming 5,000 points therefore gave me 1.92 cents per Wyndham point, about 3.5 times TPG's November 2026 valuation of 0.55 cents per Wyndham point.

Related: It’s easy to earn Wyndham Diamond status — here’s how and why you should care

I took a Lyft from downtown Kansas City, Missouri, to Riverside, a small suburb on the north bank of the Missouri River. First impressions of the property were that it was pretty remote, with nothing really nearby other than the Argosy Casino.

There was plenty of parking, and the 48 rooms were spread across a two-story motor-inn-style building.

While the property was less than 20 years old and was renovated in 2010, the rather garish lime-green lobby looked ready for another refresh.

I was quickly helped by a very friendly attendant, who I believe was the franchisee, and his wife, who also greeted me warmly.

There were several property rules listed on the counter with normal restrictions on smoking and pets in rooms.

What raised an eyebrow was the rule that visitors were allowed in guest rooms for only 60 minutes maximum, which made me wonder what kind of visitors might be passing through the doors and for what purpose in one-hour blocks.

The attendant thanked me for being a Wyndham Rewards member and quickly handed me my room key. So far, the experience had been better than the 2.8-out-of-5 rating suggested, but the room would be the biggest test.

I nervously opened the door to find a comfortable room with a king-size bed, plenty of pillows, a large flat-screen TV, a minifridge and a workspace.

Like the lobby, I doubt this decor will win any design awards, but it was clean, quiet and comfortable, and everything worked.

The separate bathroom had a tub/shower combo and a spotless toilet with several towels for me to choose from.

If I had one complaint about the room, it was that the showerhead was pulling away from the bathroom wall, but it still provided a steady flow of hot water.

The property was light on other amenities: There was no fitness center, swimming pool, bar or restaurant. However, the Argosy Casino was a few minutes' walk away, so there was plenty to keep me occupied for the evening.

After a good night's uninterrupted sleep, all guests even received a complimentary breakfast, with toast, cereals, juice and coffee available.

This is a great deal for a 5,000 point redemption with no resort fee.

Related: How I earned 24,500 points from $180 in hotel stays

The staff bid me a friendly farewell when I checked out, and I was on my way to the airport after a comfortable, peaceful and stress-free stay.

Wyndham Rewards are easy to earn, as they transfer at a 1:1 rate from the following transferable rewards:

But the best transfer option is for anyone with Wells Fargo Rewards points. This is because rather than transferring at a 1:1 rate, they transfer at a much more generous 1:2 rate. This means you would only need 2,500 Wells Fargo points to book a 5,000-point Wyndham Rewards hotel night, and Wells Fargo points can be transferred in any increments, unlike the strict 1,000-point increments of most transferable rewards.

Given that Wyndham Rewards properties offering 5,000-point nights regularly sell these nights for around $100 cash, this is an easy way to get around 4 cents per Wells Fargo point, more than twice TPG's valuation of Wells Fargo Rewards points.

Barclays also offers four Wyndham Rewards branded credit cards. Depending on the card and, in some cases, when it was opened, eligible cardholders receive a 10%, 20%, or 25% discount on free-night redemptions. That reduces a standard 5,000-point night to 4,500, 4,000 or 3,750 points, respectively.

Wyndham's new 5,000-point redemptions will not put you in a luxury hotel, but this stay was terrific value for money and delivered a clean, quiet room, a comfortable bed and a simple breakfast before an early flight.

The decor was dated, and the loose showerhead fixture needed attention. Even so, the friendly service and uninterrupted night's sleep were far better than the hotel's 2.8-out-of-5 rating had led me to expect. For a one-night stay near an airport, I would give it 4 out of 5.

Redeeming 5,000 Wyndham Rewards points instead of paying the nearly $100 member rate will give you 2 cents' worth per point. Even better, a traveler transferring from Wells Fargo Rewards would need just 2,500 points for the same award — I can't think of a more valuable way to use Wells Fargo points.

I would happily stay at a property like this again for just 5,000 Wyndham Rewards points per night.

#6122. How Many Crew Members Does It Take To Fly A B-1 Lancer?

The B-1 Lancer remains an integral part of the US Air Force’s long-range bombing capability. While the process of phasing out the supersonic variable-sweep-wing heavy bomber is underway, the aircraft is set for at least a decade more of service. This is especially true as the Air Force awaits the moment it can drop the Lancer from its ranks with absolute certainty that it will not leave a weaker fleet overall.

Reaching such a moment was always going to be tough, though. The Lancer is highly versatile, capable of carrying the largest payload of conventional weapons among any jet in the US Air Force to target precision or non-precision targets on various missions. No doubt, that is hard to replicate. It also explains why operating such an aircraft takes a whole team of crewmembers.

In total, it requires four personnel onboard to split the workload of operating the B-1 Lancer. Two pilots — an aircraft commander and co-pilot — sit up front and handle the task of getting the high-speed bomber to target, often over hours-long missions. Two personnel located behind them in the aft crew station are then responsible for managing the jet’s weapons systems.

But each crewmember’s task is complementary to another's, and their jobs are interlinked in practice. By design, the Lancer boasts multi-mission capabilities that Boeing — the primary contractor for the program since acquiring Rockwell International in 1996 — notes can be applied anywhere in the world. That means managing the Lancer’s variable wing sweeps, carrying out air-to-air refueling, and even flying low-level at high speed across variable terrain, to name a few, all before deploying weapons. That, naturally, takes a team.

While the pilots divvy up tasks like handling the Lancer and carrying out standard communications, the rear-seat weapons systems officers — or combat systems officers, as the Air Force calls them — directly offer aid in several ways. The offensive systems officer (OSO) is responsible for navigation, as well as primarily operating the plane’s Lockheed Martin targeting system known as a Sniper Pod, for instance. Including a defensive systems officer (DSO) who monitors threats and might deploy countermeasures, the rear-seaters also assist during low-flying by calling out altimeter readings, for example. Each weapons systems officer is trained to do the other's jobs too, and can communicate with ground forces to coordinate strikes. Again, it takes a crew to fly the Lancer, and that is partly down to its extensive capabilities.

Alongside the B-52 Stratofortress and B-2 Spirit, the B-1 Lancer is one of three bomber types the US Air Force uses today. Accordingly, each has a specific role. The B-52 is the heaviest of the trio and the backbone of the fleet by number in service. Conversely, the stealth B-2 is designed to penetrate air defenses. Each of these can be equipped with nuclear, as well as conventional weapons. While the B-1 only carries conventional payloads, it is arguably the most versatile.

Indeed, the B-1 trumps its counterparts in range and service ceiling, as detailed below in figures from the Washington DC-based industry publication The National Interest. Notably, it is the quickest of the three, being the only one capable of surpassing supersonic speeds. It also boasts the highest maximum payload, at roughly 75,000 pounds (34,000 kg) compared with the B-52’s approximate 70,000 pounds (31,500 kg) and the B-2’s maximum 40,000 pounds (18,100 kg).

US Air Force bombers, from The National Interest:

~79 feet swept / ~137 feet extended (24/41.8 meters)

1,620-3,780 nautical miles (3,000-7,000 km)

~70,000 pounds (31,500 kg) of mixed ordnance, including conventional bombs, precision-guided munitions, stand-off weapons, and nuclear weapons

~75,000 pounds (34,000 kg) of conventional weapons

Up to 40,000 pounds (18,100 kg) of conventional and nuclear precision munitions

Developed in the 1970s, the B-1 was initially slated to replace the B-52. Some to-and-fro saw the program canceled in 1977; however, it was reinstated under the Reagan administration, at which point improvements were made and the B-1B variant we know today emerged. As the Air Force writes: “[Its] capabilities, when combined with its substantial payload, excellent radar targeting system, long loiter time, and survivability, make the B-1B a key element of any joint or composite strike force.”

The B-52 stays relevant thanks to its low operating costs, its plentiful remaining flight hours, and the ability to use stand-off munitions.

In any case, getting a B-1 Lancer off the ground takes far more than just its four-strong flight crew. Behind the scenes, everything from refueling to major fixes can pile on the human hours required to keep just one of the jets in service.

The 28th Maintenance Group, responsible for servicing B-1s at Ellsworth Air Force Base, South Dakota, and one of the jet’s two primary stations, is said to encompass some 1,500 professionals, for reference. This is split into four squadrons, each supplying personnel for specific work — be it loading and supporting mission operations, servicing munitions, managing overall fleet utilization and health, or carrying out heavy repairs.

While a flight crew rested, ate, checked out equipment, received several briefings, and so on before a mission during Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan, ground-based maintenance crews regularly spent five or more hours preparing each B-1, per the Air Force. That is, the entire aircraft was analyzed to be cleared to fly by a crew chief. Upon each B-1’s return, about 10 maintenance specialists would meet the flight crew for a briefing on the plane’s performance, before an intelligence officer sat down with those onboard to go over the mission details. While substantial, the large-scale effort required for each B-1 flight is similarly mirrored by its counterparts.

As the largest US bomber in operation today, the B-52 Stratofortress also requires the largest aircrew. No doubt that's also down to its roots dating back to the 1950s, and to older technology that relies on several specialist operators. In contrast, the B-2 Spirit is operated with a smaller, more conventional crew than both the B-52 and B-1.

For the B-52, five personnel go on each mission, including an aircraft commander, co-pilot, and electronic warfare officer—all seated on the upper deck—alongside a radar navigator and a navigator located downstairs. Add in those on the ground and the number needed per flight balloons once again. The 5th Mission Support Group — one of five groups assigned to support B-52 operations from Minot Air Force Base, North Dakota — has 1,600 military and civilian members alone, for instance, though it also serves the 91st Missile Wing.

Just two crew members are needed to operate the far more modern B-2, developed in the 1980s and first delivered in 1993. This includes a pilot and mission commander. They are also joined by numerous people on the ground, with the 509th Bomb Wing at Whiteman Air Force Base, Missouri, again encompassing several groups dedicated to supporting B-2 operations at one of two sites that primarily house the bomber.

Such a two-strong crew makeup, like that of the B-2 Spirit, is on course to become increasingly common across the US Air Force’s bomber fleet. With the Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider set to start arriving with the military from next year, existing B-2s and B-1 Lancers will make way.

This process has already begun, in fact. In 2021, it was announced that 17 B-1s would be retired, leaving an active fleet of 45. “Due to the wear and tear placed on the B-1 fleet over the past two decades, maintaining these bombers would cost tens of millions of dollars per aircraft to get back to status quo,” then Air Force Global Strike Command head Timothy Ray said at the time. “And that’s just to fix the problems we know about.”

Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider specifications, from The Defense Post:

Those that are left are expected to be retained into the 2030s to ensure time for the new B-21 fleet to be delivered and incorporated. Given that plans are for the Air Force to acquire at least 100 of the new stealth bombers, extensive training of flight and maintenance crews will be needed, of course.

Either way, that means the B-1 Lancer’s days are somewhat numbered, along with its unique four-person aircrew requirement. As to when the B-1 will ultimately be phased out, time will tell. Plans previously called for this to happen in the early 2030s. Now it is expected to be closer to the end of the decade.

In the meantime, funds are still being poured into sustaining and modernizing what is left of the fleet. Back in 2019, Boeing secured a $14.2 billion contract to test and modify weapons systems on both B-1 Lancers and B-52 Stratofortresses.

#6121. Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

“If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”

In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

#6120. Norse Atlantic Cancels All Flights, Will File For Bankruptcy

Just days after warning that its financial situation was “critical,” Norse Atlantic Airways appears to have reached the end of the line.

The low-cost carrier said Monday that its main Norwegian operating unit will file for bankruptcy. All flights were canceled, and ticket sales were discontinued.

Despite “extensive efforts,” the company was unable to secure financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs, officials said. The board of directors “concluded that there is no longer a basis for continued operations” for the Norwegian business.

A bankruptcy petition is expected to be filed Monday with Agder District Court in Norway.

Other parts of the company, including Norse Atlantic UK, could be restructured and continue operating, but no firm plans have been announced.

“We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees, and partners,” CEO Eivind Roald said in a statement. “The board, management, and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the U.K. subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations.”

Norse Atlantic operated only long-haul international flights, connecting cities such as Oslo, New York, Stockholm, Rome, Cape Town, Orlando, Florida, and Phuket, Thailand. That business model became unsustainable as the war in Iran pushed jet fuel prices higher.

The carrier said earlier this year that it was contemplating a sale, but no partner was ever announced. On Wednesday, it warned that its financial situation was “critical,” and said short-term financing was needed immediately to keep operations going.
