Although the holiday season can be joyous, it can be an expensive time of year, with gifts, travel and gatherings putting extra pressure on your budget.

But with a little planning, you can make the most of your credit card rewards and benefits without overspending.

Here are five tips to help you save money and earn rewards like a pro this holiday season.

First, map out your holiday shopping plans and set a realistic budget for spending. Who are you shopping for? How much are you planning to spend on gifts? What other expenses should you factor into your holiday budget?

These are all good questions to help you set expectations and prevent impulse buys that can lead to overspending.

A spreadsheet is a great way to keep track of spending and budgeting. You can simply insert your budget into a premade template or write it down on paper. If you already know what you plan to buy, insert links to the sales pages so you know how much it will cost.

While adjusting and finalizing your budget, remember to factor in additional costs due to extra gatherings, like larger grocery and dining expenses.

One of the best things about rewards cards is that they often come with perks to help you save money.

Before making your holiday purchases, check whether your credit cards offer statement credits or other benefits that could help you save money.

For example, comes with an up to $75 quarterly statement credit (up to $300 annually) Lululemon credit that can be used at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) or online after enrollment. This is a great way to maximize purchases on clothing, yoga gear or other accessories.

Or, if you have a frequent jet-setter in your life, you can use a credit card’s Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit to cover their application fee of up to $120.

Statement credits aren't the only card benefits worth checking before you shop. For an expensive electronic device or other high-value gift, purchase protection or extended warranty coverage are other useful perks.

We talk a lot about shopping portals during this time of year. That's because skipping them is essentially leaving money on the table.

By doing your online holiday shopping through a portal, you can earn bonus points or cash back at a massive number of online retailers. Most of the major U.S. airlines have shopping portals to help you earn additional miles on every eligible purchase, or you can use third-party portals such as Rakuten to earn cash back or Amex Membership Rewards or Bilt Points.

We suggest using a shopping portal aggregator like Cashback Monitor to find the best portal for each online purchase. That way, you don’t have to sift through each portal’s offers individually.

No matter where you shop, review any Amex Offers, Chase Offers or Citi Merchant Offers available on your cards. They vary by cardmember, and often stack with your card's standard rewards plus a shopping portal. Some require activation or enrollment before making a purchase.

Related: Everything you need to know about credit card merchant offers

We’re big fans of points and miles at The Points Guy — and for good reason. Points and miles can reduce the cost of future travel, but cash-back cards may be more useful if you want rewards to offset your holiday expenses directly.

A flat-rate cash-back card such as the (see rates and fees) is an easy way to earn rewards no matter where you shop since it offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase and another 1% cash back when you pay your bill. Redeeming those rewards as a statement credit helps reduce the size of January's bill.

The (see rates and fees) is another great option that earns at least 1.5% back on every purchase.

Paying your statement balance in full is generally best, but some rewards credit cards offer a 0% introductory annual percentage rate period on new purchases. That can give you time to pay for a planned expense without interest as long as you have a plan to pay it off completely before the introductory period ends.

Another option is to use one of the financing options some credit card issuers offer. Amex Plan It® and Chase Pay Over Time after purchase may allow eligible cardmembers to divide qualifying purchases of $100 or more into fixed monthly payments, generally with a fixed monthly fee instead of interest.

You’ll almost always save money using these programs compared to paying interest over time.

Related: Chase Pay Over Time and My Chase Loan: Should you opt in?

Holiday shopping doesn't have to derail your budget. By planning ahead, using the right rewards cards and taking advantage of statement credits and shopping portals, you can make your spending more rewarding without buying more than you can afford.

The key is to prioritize your budget over earning points, miles or cash back. After all, the value of those rewards can quickly disappear if you're carrying a balance and paying interest.

#6116. Restored to Calder’s plan, the clouds are spinning again

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

Fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

“It’s totally phenomenal,” he said, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”

It was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

Rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”

“It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”

It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

“We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he said. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”

Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and said he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

“We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he said. “Nobody got how big this was until it showed up on their doorstep.”

Quilici said he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

“Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

“This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most important and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement said.

The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

“It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” said Kim Shirley.

In addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

But when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and said he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

“Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

According to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The new clouds, he said, are made of carbon fiber.

“These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he said.

Younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

“I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

“I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he said, gazing up at it.

#6115. United Sends 3 Jets To Fly 500 Stranded Texas Students Home After Storm Derails Macy's Parade

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

United Airlines has stepped in to help the Pride of Pearland Band and Color Guard to travel home from New York to Texas, after the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed. This came as the parade was postponed for the first time in the parade's 100-year history, due to a severe coastal storm that was forecast to impact New York City.

The new parade has been rescheduled from Thursday, November 26, to Saturday, November 28, with kickoff expected at 8:30 AM EST. These last-minute changes have affected thousands of participants' travel plans, and for the Pearland Band and Color Guard, from Pearland High School in Pearland, Texas, United has stepped in with three dedicated aircraft to transport the members and their chaperones home.

As reported by Click2Houston, the community from Pearland, Texas came together to raise $350,000 that was required to keep the high school's band and Guard in New York due to the postponement of the parade. The former Pearland Mayor, Kevin Cole, led the effort to ensure all students in the group could remain in New York, and Star Alliance carrier United has now stepped in to ensure everyone will get home safely.

Initially, there was a plan to bring all participants home by bus, due to existing flight availability only providing options on Monday or Tuesday. Following support from United, all members will now get to fly home on Saturday evening.

Simple Flying reached out to United for comment on this support to Pearland High School on Saturday morning; however, an airline spokesperson could not immediately be reached.

The three extra flights put on by United are set to depart on Saturday from LaGuardia (LGA) and Newark (EWR). These will arrive back into Houston Intercontinental (IAH) between 9:30 PM and 11:00 PM local time. Each plane will carry approximately 170 travelers back to Texas. Members of the Pearland community have also been invited to gather at Pearland High School to welcome back the group.

With the severe weather conditions affecting Thanksgiving Day Parade plans in New York, this led to the extraordinary decision to postpone the event for the first time in a century, due to high winds exceeding the safety thresholds that are needed to permit the flying of giant balloons. The only three other times that have seen cancelations or operational changes included:

The parade was suspended during World War II when rubber and other materials that would otherwise be used for balloons were redirected for the war effort.

Adverse weather conditions resulted in organizers grounding the giant balloons due to strong winds.

In the midst of the COVID-19 Pandemic, the parade was broadcast on television without on-site spectators. This saw heavy filming and staffing changes.

For the members of the Pearland Band and Color Guard and their chaperones, the decision by United to support the group back to Texas came as a welcome relief to fly in a matter of hours, instead of what would have been in excess of 24 hours on a bus.

United Airlines is expanding in Cleveland with new Las Vegas and Miami flights, but its return signals a new strategy, not a restored hub.

With many other groups affected by the postponement of the Thanksgiving Day Parade, this has left many struggling to change travel plans. As reported by the Star Advertiser, this included the 200-member Na Koa Alii Hawaii All-State Marching Band from the state of Hawaii. This sudden change saw the group looking for donations, and they were able to raise $500,000 in a matter of hours.

Hawaiian and Alaska Airlines stepped in on Thursday evening, announcing that they would help support the group and its chaperones' trip home to Hawaii. The group will travel from New York to Seattle (SEA), before connecting onto flights back to Hawaii.

The once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for many to participate in the 100th edition of the parade has made much of the sudden postponement all worth it. The Na Koa Alii Hawaii All-State Marching Band and Pride of Pearland Band and Color Guard are two of nine marching bands that are set to appear in the parade.

#6114. Orient Express Sailing Yachts Review: Corinthian’s Suites, Dining, Amenities, Service, And More

Orient Express Sailing Yachts voyages are best booked through Accor Preferred travel advisors. They can get you the best price, and also add a shipboard credit. Ford and his team are happy to help with any requests, and can be reached at [email protected].

For the main event of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, Ford and I had the chance to spend four nights on the Corinthian, which is the first ship in Orient Express’ new cruising venture, known as Orient Express Sailing Yachts.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts set sail in the summer of 2026, and with just 54 suites that can accommodate up to 110 guests, it really brings luxury cruising to a new level. It’s a fascinating time for the luxury cruising industry more broadly, given how competition has been heating up.

I also recently reviewed Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, and had a great experience, and reviewed Four Seasons Yachts, which is definitely more luxurious, but also has some growing pains. Lastly, I’ve compared all the experiences as well.

While Orient Express Sailing Yachts is the highest priced cruising venture to date, I have to say, the experience really is unbelievably good, and at least you feel like you’re getting an amazing experience. I come into these kinds of trips with a critical eye, and I was just blown away by the ship’s design, the quality of the food and drinks, and the service. To me the ship felt like a step back in time (in terms of its classic elegance), while also being cutting edge modern.

If you can swing this experience, I’d highly recommend it. Okay, enough of an intro, here comes my 8,500-word review (yikes, this is the longest review I’ve ever published of anything).

Orient Express Sailing Yachts charges per suite (rather than per person, based on double occupancy), and you’ll find that journeys typically cost an average of $4,000-6,000 per cabin per night for a base suite. Make no mistake, this is the very top end of the cruise market, and at this point you’re paying safari prices for the experience.

Let me also emphasize that rates go up from there, and Orient Express Sailing Yachts has some of the most insane suites you’ll find at sea, some of which can cost six figures per sailing. Currently, Orient Express offers cruises in Europe in summer, and in the Caribbean in winter, with transatlantic sailings in the spring and fall.

For what it’s worth, you’ll find rate parity regardless of which booking channel you reserve through. So your best bet is to book through a travel advisor affiliated with Accor Preferred, because they can add perks to your journey. The size of the credit depends on the accommodation type booked, plus the length of the journey. Ford and his team are of course happy to help with these bookings, and can be reached at [email protected].

In the interest of full disclosure, Ford was invited on this Orient Express Sailing Yachts journey (due to the amount of volume he books), and I tagged along with him. All opinions expressed are my own, and I plan to review this exactly the same way I reviewed the two previous cruises (which we paid full price for). I haven’t been asked to write anything, and I have no incentive to be anything other than honest. If people are going to drop a ton of money on a luxury cruise, I want to make sure they’re at least getting the best experience possible.

We experienced Orient Express Sailing Yachts in early October 2026, shortly before the ship’s transatlantic sailing. Admittedly it wasn’t the most exciting itinerary, but that’s just what worked out for us in terms of timing, since we wanted to minimize our time away from home, had to schedule it around when family could best be with our kids, etc. Below is the itinerary for the sailing we took.

We were happy with this itinerary, since our primary goal was to see the ship. It definitely wasn’t the most exciting, though, given that we docked at the port in Mahón (rather than tendering), and it also meant we didn’t have a marina day (not that you’d necessarily want that in October, since it’s a bit chillier). But the point is that if you’re traveling more in peak season, you can expect a marina day more consistently.

Historically, cruising has been all about offering an all-inclusive experience. That’s true with Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, but then Four Seasons Yachts countered the trend, by only including breakfast, and then charging extra for lunch, dinner, and drinks (I don’t love this concept, especially given the quality issues they have).

While Orient Express Sailing Yachts might charge a lot, what I really appreciate is how the company has an ultra all-inclusive concept, to an extent that’s even greater than you’ll find on most other cruise lines. Orient Express Sailing Yachts journeys include the following:

Orient Express Sailing Yachts journeys don’t include the following:

Regarding the Orient Express Sailing Yachts tipping policy, the company states that gratuities are included in the fare — “however, if you wish to offer a tip as an extra gesture of appreciation, it will be warmly received.”

I just have to emphasize that the level of inclusions really impressed me. Seriously, I was served caviar with breakfast, lunch, and dinner at various points (and even cocktails!), and the house champagne is Veuve Clicquot La Grande Dame 2018 (which retails for around $200 per bottle).

Orient Express Sailing Yachts currently has a single ship, which is named the Corinthian (a second ship is being introduced in 2027, and it’ll be named the Olympian).

The ship entered service in 2026, and is 722 feet (220 meters) long, 82 feet (25 meters) wide, and 26,600 gross tons. With 54 accommodations and a maximum capacity of around 110 guests, there’s a roughly 1.5:1 staff to guest ratio, given that there are around 170 staff onboard. The spaciousness of this ship, and the amount of space allocated to each passenger, really is next level.

The Corinthian also has the title of being the world’s largest sailing yacht, as it has three automated SolidSail rigid sails on tilting carbon masts, to provide wind propulsion, alongside hybrid LNG auxiliary power. It’s just such an elegant and distinctive looking ship, that it can’t help but turn heads. For those curious, it was explained that the sails reduce emissions by around 10%, and no, the ship doesn’t “heel” in the way a smaller sailboat would. Unless you’re looking up, you wouldn’t realize there are even sails.

You can find the full Corinthian deck plan here. As you’d expect for a sail boat, there aren’t quite as many floors as on a traditional cruise ship. Guests can access a total of five floors, between levels three and seven. To briefly cover that:

Near the ship’s entrance, you’ll find a very cool directory of sorts, which shows the floorplan of the ship. You can click any amenity, and then it will light up, so that’s super handy.

The ship has two sets of elevator banks, as well as two sets of staircases, so getting around the ship is really easy. We always used the stairs, since we were typically within a couple of floors of where we needed to be.

As you’d expect, the ease of boarding a ship varies greatly depending on its size, but Orient Express Sailing Yachts really took it to the next level in terms of how seamless it was. We had spent a night at the Hôtel Dieu Intercontinental Marseille. Our journey included the transfers, so an Orient Express representative met us at the hotel, and then we were driven to the port.

Getting onboard the ship literally couldn’t have been easier. There were no formalities in the port, but instead, we were escorted straight through security, and then check-in was handled once onboard.

There were no other guests as we boarded, and the staff really went above and beyond — for example, the crew member who escorted us through security and onto the ship insisted on holding an umbrella over our heads, to shade us from the sun.

Our check-in process onboard took all of five minutes, and at that point we were introduced to our butler, Reuben, who escorted us to our suite, and took care of everything from there. I should mention how Reuben was German, so they specifically appointed us a German butler, which I thought was super fun (so we communicated with him exclusively in German).

We didn’t have a stop that involved tendering, but for those situations where you do, it’s an efficient process, given how few guests there are. Our one stop had us docked in port, and there was a nice seating area outside the ship with bottled water, sunscreen, etc. Admittedly a setup like this is more useful when you’re waiting on a tender, rather than just walking directly onto or off the ship.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts has 54 suites onboard, spread across over a dozen different categories. The entry level suites here are among the most spacious at sea, while the penthouse suites really take luxury and space to the next level.

Our sailing was rather empty — only 19 of the 54 suites were occupied — and we were upgraded to a higher suite category (I believe they had blocked most of the entry level room categories, as they were doing some minor updates to them ahead of the ship heading to the Caribbean). So let me share my thoughts on that suite first, and then I’ll share some pictures of other suites that I had the opportunity to tour as well.

We stayed in an Appartement Prestige, which is one of the more premium standard suite categories, but below the duplex suites and penthouse suites. These suites are marketed as being an average of 1,119 square feet (104 square meters), so they’re incredibly spacious.

We were assigned suite 518, located on the fifth floor. The hallways on the Corinthian are just stunning, as you can see below. It really feels more like a luxury hotel than a ship, especially in terms of the width of the hallway.

The concept of forgetting that one is on a ship continued inside the suite. The interior felt more to me like a “Palace” hotel in France, than what you’d expect at sea. I can’t even imagine how much money was spent on the interiors, as the quality of the finishes, from the wall treatments to the carpet, as well as the furniture, was just unreal.

Upon entering the suite, there was first a dining area with a table and a chair, as well as a desk with a chair (that chair could also be moved over to the dining table). It’s not often you get this kind of space in a cruise ship suite.

The minibar was also in this area, and was well stocked, with everything being complimentary. This included a Nespresso coffee machine, cocktails, wine, beer, soft drinks, etc. They were also happy to replenish the minibar however you wanted, so there are really no limits.

That entry area then flowed into the living room, which was gorgeous. It had a couch and a coffee table, as well as a hidden TV (which would pop up from in front of the mirror).

Waiting on the dining table was a lovely welcome amenity, consisting of some freshly baked treats, a fruit plate, and a bottle of Veuve Clicquot 2015 Rose. There was also an Orient Express branded journal, along with two Orient Express water bottles, which guests could take home.

Double doors then led into the bedroom, which had a very plush king size bed.

Much like with the bedroom, the bathroom will make you forget that you’re on a ship, as it had double sinks, a soaking tub, a walk-in shower with amazing water pressure, and a toilet in a separate room.

There were also a couple of closet areas, so there was plenty of space to store luggage and clothes.

The suite then had a balcony that stretched the entire length of the suite, with very comfortable furniture.

Beyond the generally beautiful design, it has to be pointed out just how over the top everything was. I mean, the deck furniture uses fabrics from Loro Piana, just to give you a sense of just how high-end it is.

Housekeeping in the room was great (it was taken care of twice daily, and always well timed), butler service was very useful (more on that a bit later, when I talk about service), Starlink Wi-Fi was lightning fast, and I also love how Orient Express Sailing Yachts includes laundry. You could get unlimited washing, dry cleaning, etc., so that’s a very nice feature.

In the interest of checking out different suite products, I also had the chance to tour the Suite Panoramique, which is the entry level accommodation onboard, located on levels four and five. These are 506 square feet (47 square meters), so they’re spacious for an entry level suite on a cruise.

This had the same general design concept as the suite we were in, except there wasn’t a fully separate living area. The suite had a comfortable king size bed, a desk with a chair, a dining table, and a huge window with a double daybed of sorts.

While there was no bathtub, the bathroom still had double sinks, a walk-in shower, and a toilet in a separate room.

To point out the obvious, these entry level suites don’t have balconies. Of course people prefer to have balconies, but this is just a simple reality of the difference between sailboats and cruise ships, in terms of how many levels there are, how far above water they are, etc.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ top end suites are really next level, so I also had the chance to tour the Zephyr Suite, which is located on level seven, and is the second most premium suite onboard. This two bedroom suite has 2,486 square feet (231 square meters) of interior space, plus a terrace that’s 1,206 square feet (112 square meters).

What I thought was so cool was how unique the design of this suite was, as the top suite products seem to have a totally original design. This very much had a residential vibe, with a long hallway connecting the various parts of the suite.

However, perhaps the coolest feature was the replica of an Orient Express Heritage cabin, intended to pay homage to the legendary train.

The Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian has two pools onboard, with one being rather traditional, and one being unlike anything else at sea (at least to my knowledge). The main “leisure” pool is located on the fifth floor, at the back of the ship. While the pool has beautiful aesthetics and lovely deck space around it, this isn’t some destination pool in and of itself. So if a huge pool is a crucial factor in picking a ship, Four Seasons Yachts might be a better option.

We’re all different, and personally, I’m not much of a pool person. Quite to the contrary, I actually loved this pool deck, since it was mostly covered and in the shade, so I could nicely sit there and enjoy the breeze (funny enough, Four Seasons Yachts has an amazing pool, but I didn’t actually spend much time there, due to the lack of shade).

The ship then has a second pool, which is among the most memorable you’ll find on any ship. The lap pool is 54 feet (16 meters) long, and it’s located under the sails. It really feels like you’re in a cave, since it’s on a deck that’s one level down from the main upper deck. What a pool!

On the pool front, really my only disappointment was the lack of a hot tub. As much as I find hot tubs to be kind of gross, I do love them, especially on a ship, so I was sad there wasn’t one of those. In general, the newer ultra high end cruise lines seem to be lacking in that department (the same was true on Four Seasons Yachts).

Beyond the pool setup, on the seventh floor you’ll find a huge deck you can hang out on. There are lots of lounge chairs out here, though it’s not necessarily that popular for just lounging around. The star of the show here is what’s above.

The time when the deck really gets popular is when the ship pulls into or out of ports, given the panoramic views from up here, plus the ability to watch the sails be lowered and raised. I must say, it was absolutely mesmerizing to watch. They made a big event of departures, with live music, cocktails, etc. It really felt like a cocktail reception, only more intimate.

Speaking of deck space, another fun aspect of the ship is how you can actually just freely walk up to the deck in front of the bridge, and even all the way to the bow. How fun!

The Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian wellness complex is located on the fourth floor, and that includes a Guerlain Spa. This area is an impressive 5,380 square feet (500 square meters), with four treatment suites (including a double suite), as well as all kinds of other traditional spa facilities.

Guests can always use the facilities, even without an appointment, and that includes a sauna, steam room, relaxation area, locker rooms, etc.

The spa treatment rooms are absolutely gorgeous, whether we’re talking about the couples room, or the individual ones.

Ford and I got a couples massage during our final day (where we were at sea), and I can honestly say it was one of the best spa treatments I’ve ever had. Not only was the therapist I had incredible, but the massage bed was so comfortable, and there was something so calming about the view, the gentle sway of the ship, etc.

For those curious about the pricing, you can find part of the spa menu below.

The ship also has a full hair salon and barber shop, so there are no shortage of opportunities to get your grooming needs taken care of here. The barber shop even leads to the speakeasy — more on that later.

The Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian has a gym located on the fourth floor, which can be accessed by guests 24/7. The gym isn’t huge, but is more than sufficient given the size of the ship, in my opinion. Every time we used it, we were alone.

The gym had a good selection of cardio and weight equipment, as well as a separate room for aerobics, boxing, etc.

There was an excellent personal trainer onboard, and it was possible to schedule sessions with him at no extra cost. So it’s not just for group fitness, but even for personal sessions, on a space available basis. That’s really nice, as virtually any other cruise would charge for that, in my experience.

The Orient Express Sailing Yachts Corinthian has an incredibly impressive entertainment area, located on deck four. The issue is, it’s not really used a whole lot. Now, I’m not sure I’d actually call this an “issue,” but let me explain.

When you think of mega cruise ships, nightly shows and entertainment are among the most popular attractions. The thing is, the smaller the ship is, the less interest there is in things like this, and that’s especially true for the cruise lines that are primarily targeted at people who haven’t historically been cruisers.

So the Corinthian has a huge theater with dozens of seats, but there’s not a whole lot that goes on there.

Perhaps the more interesting entertainment feature is the private cinema, where you can have them screen a movie (or whatever) for you.

There’s even a recording studio onboard — what a cool concept, and in addition to being able to play instruments here, I heard people have used this to record podcasts, etc.

On the topic of entertainment, the ship also has a card room on the fourth floor, with chess, checkers, decks of cards, etc.

Separately, there’s also the yacht club, which is basically a very elegant lounge area where guests can hang out, watch TV, etc.

Lastly, the ship has the library on the fourth floor, which has an incredible selection of books. Everything on the Corinthian is so thoughtful, including the book selection. As it was explained to us, the 1,500-book library is supposed to represent the most important books of the century, and were curated by the historic Parisian bookshop Galignani.

I know there’s sometimes confusion about whether Orient Express Sailing Yachts is kids friendly, and the answer is… sort of.

On most voyages, guests onboard must be 16 years of age or older. However, on dedicated family voyages, children ages six months to 15 years old are allowed as well. Infants under six months aren’t permitted onboard, and per the terms, “families traveling with little ones under two years old must be accompanied by a dedicated babysitter throughout their voyage.”

Quite honestly, it’s logical that Orient Express Sailing Yachts would have this policy, since the ship’s venues feel really intimate, the pools aren’t huge, etc.

For family voyages, the Corinthian does have a kids club onboard, which offers activities with a dedicated team. Babysitting services can also be arranged for excursions or gala evenings. But in terms of being kids friendly, I definitely think it’s an area where Four Seasons Yachts wins, as all voyages are kids friendly, the pool is huge, and there’s both a kids club and teens club.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts has an incredibly impressive selection of restaurants, bars, and lounges onboard, with the culinary vision overseen by well-known chef Yannick Alléno. Before I get into details, let me just say that I found the quality of food and drinks onboard to be truly exceptional.

I try not to exaggerate, because I think far too many people are a little too generous when describing food on cruises (or flights, for that matter — what’s with all these people describing airplane food as Michelin dining?). However, I found the quality of catering on Orient Express Sailing Yachts to just be in a completely different league than Four Seasons Yachts.

I was also delighted by the generosity of the included options, with an incredible alcohol selection, caviar accompanying dishes at breakfast, lunch, and dinner (and even cocktails), etc. It’s also interesting to note that no reservations are allowed onboard, except at the fine dining restaurant that costs extra.

Everything was always available whenever we wanted it, though people will otherwise probably have mixed feelings on that policy (conversely, the issue when you do allow reservations is that people hog them and then just cancel at the last minute, leaving other guests with limited options).

Anyway, here are the most significant outlets onboard Orient Express Sailing Yachts:

With that out of the way, let’s get into the venues in a bit more detail.

La Terrasse is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ all-day dining restaurant, serving breakfast, lunch, and dinner. It’s located at the back of the sixth floor, and has both indoor and outdoor seating. The fact that this is the casual restaurant really tells you the quality of the experience, as there are white tablecloths all hours of the day.

This is the primary restaurant where breakfast is served, and you can find that menu below.

Breakfast is entirely a la carte, though at the start of the meal, a basket with a rotating selection of croissants and pastries was brought out.

There was a large selection of fresh juices and coffee available. My one disappointment was that the coffee was just okay, and clearly came from a machine. That’s ironic, because there’s plenty of delicious barista coffee on the ship, so this seems to be one of the only venues where that’s the case. Given the quality of service onboard, I’m sure they’d also be happy to get you a coffee from somewhere else, if you prefer.

We found the breakfast selection to be very good, and over the course of our stay tried the acai bowl with coconut and seasonal fruit, chia pudding with fresh mango, the mixed berry plate, the crispy and soft blinis with caviar cream and smoked salmon, the avocado toast, and more.

We also came to La Terrasse one day for lunch, and you can find that menu below.

We split the chickpea hummus with parmesan to start, and then had the smoked salmon club sandwich and Thai beef salad as our mains. At our server’s insistence, we finished off with a floating island for dessert. YUM.

We also had dinner here our first evening, and you can find that menu below.

To start, we had the smoked salmon with blinis and sour cream, and the gazpacho.

Then for mains, we had the pepper crusted beef fillet with cognac and cream sauce, and the red tuna teriyaki style, along with some sides.

Lastly, we finished off the meal with a selection from the cheese trolley, plus the vanilla millefeuille.

Across the board, the food and service were exceptional, so it’s amazing that this is just the most basic restaurant onboard, as it only gets better from there.

L’Ecrin is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ elevated dinner restaurant, with a focus on seafood and pasta. It’s located on the sixth floor, and it exclusively has indoor seating. This restaurant doesn’t cost extra, but in my opinion is on par with the paid restaurant on some of the other top ships.

We went here one evening for dinner, and you can find the menu below.

At the start of the meal, we were offered some sinfully delicious bread, along with some cured meats. I’ll talk more about service in a bit, but I might as well just mention in passing how good the crew was about our dietary preferences. For example, we mentioned when we boarded how we don’t eat pork, so without having to say anything, we were brought something that fit our needs.

We took an unusual approach to ordering. To start, we shared the seabass carpaccio with citrus marinade, and the spaghetti with caviar. My gosh, not only was the caviar portion on the spaghetti massive, but the overall flavor of the dish was incredible, as the beurre blanc combined with caviar had quite the unique flavor profile.

Then for mains, we had the warm lobster with olive oil and mayonnaise and the caponata and polenta. Again, this was very, very good.

For dessert, while I had heard amazing things about the suzette pasta (flambeed tableside), we decided on the signature bronte pistachio ice cream coupe, which was insanely indulgent.

What a meal! This was definitely my favorite restaurant onboard.

La Table by Yannick Alléno is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ most premium dinner restaurant, and it’s the only venue that comes at an extra charge, at the rate of €400 per person for the tasting menu.

First, we have to talk about the restaurant as such. Can you believe this is on a ship? This is without a doubt the most beautiful dining venue I’ve ever seen on a ship. With just over half a dozen tables, it’s also a really intimate space.

The tasting menu is constantly changing, and you can find the menu for our dinner below.

I’ll let the pictures speak for themselves…

The meal was very good, with service that matched the food quality. It really felt like a Michelin-starred dining experience in terms of the presentation, the service flow, etc.

While this was excellent, I will say, I wouldn’t necessarily feel compelled to dine here again. That’s just because the standard restaurants are so great that I don’t necessarily think it’s worth the incremental cost. At a minimum, don’t feel like you’re missing out if you don’t eat here… but definitely do take a look at the restaurant, to appreciate its beauty!

L’Encre is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ venue that’s exclusively open for lunch, and it was definitely my favorite lunch spot onboard. It’s basically a circular counter with a little over a dozen seats, so the setting is stunning.

You can find the menu below. Think of the concept as basically being like a seafood omakase, where they just keep bringing you out more dishes. Of course you can customize however you want, ask for more of whatever you really like, skip dishes, etc. Below is a sampling of what we ate.

La Piscine Lounge is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ poolside venue, serving drinks, snacks, and even full meals, throughout most of the day. It’s even opening at night, and can double as a bar for a pre-dinner drink. It’s a beautiful space, definitely not your typical pool bar!

You can find the drink list and menu for that below.

We had an afternoon snack here one day, and split the mezze and the veggie burger, both of which were very good.

Le Bar de la Bibliotheque is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ coffee shop in the library area, and it’s a lovely place from which to get some work done, read a book, etc.

Here you’ll find barista coffee, homemade cakes, fresh juices, kombucha, and more.

Le Wagon Bar is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ primary bar venue, and it’s only open late at night. It’s intended to be a replica of the circular bar found on the modern Orient Express trains, with 1920s and 1930s heritage craftsmanship, so it’s a very cool space.

There’s a DJ there at night. The one thing to be aware of is that it only opens really late (9:30PM at the earliest, but often 10PM), and if you’re on a quieter sailing, there might not be too much of a vibe here. However, I’ve heard that on other sailings this place can be packed — it’s all about the crowd on a particular cruise.

I ordered the signature Corinthian Martini, with gin, vodka, champagne cordial, and — naturally, like everything on this ship — caviar!

Next, Le Speakeasy Bar is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ speakeasy. The idea is basically that people do a bar crawl, and it’s common to move between both bars in the same evening. Much like Le Wagon Bar, this one also opens really late.

The bar is located through a hidden door in the barbershop, so they’re really committed to that speakeasy theme.

This bar even has a separate smoking room, which I’m sure smokers will appreciate (as it’s the only indoor space on the ship where you can smoke).

This bar also has some unique signature cocktails, and you can find that drink list below.

While not included, they are very proud of their liquor selection here, with some bottles that are older than my dad (and at a cost of up to $2,400 per shot — yowzers!).

Tempted as I was, I stuck to one of the included martinis. 😉

Le Flybridge Bar is Orient Express Sailing Yachts’ outdoor bar space located on the top floor. While this is open quite frequently, it really only gets busy when the ship sets sail, given the interest in watching the sails in action.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts of course has 24/7 room service, which is included, with no additional costs. The standard room service menu is on the basic side, but service very much falls into the category of them wanting to make guests happy, so they’re also happy to get you something from any restaurant, if you’d like (but since the menus are always changing, they’re not published in the room service menu).

We did have room service dinner one evening…

…and the final morning we had breakfast in our suite as well (we accidentally ordered too much).

Our amazing butler, Reuben, also gladly brought us cappuccinos and protein shakes, so they were happy to accommodate guests however they could.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts has a very impressive included drink menu. You can find the standard alcoholic drink list below, though some venues have additional options or signature cocktails customized to that venue.

Having Veuve Clicquot La Grande Dame 2018 as the house champagne is very impressive. And let me just say, they’re also not cheap with the pours — you can barely go anywhere without having a glass pushed on you. 😉

Of course there’s also a premium drink list with even more special wines and spirits, and those come at an extra cost.

I have to acknowledge that our sailing was rather empty, so the staff to guest ratio on this sailing was unreal. That being said, it wasn’t just the ratio that was amazing, but the quality of staff was really incredible as well. If you don’t have good staff, they’ll find a way to disappoint even if the staff to guest ratio is amazing.

I’m not exaggerating when I say that service on Orient Express Sailing Yachts was flawless in terms of attention to detail, and that was such a contrast to our Four Seasons Yachts experience.

It’s hard to even pinpoint any one area that impressed me, because it was just very consistent, polished, and proactive, across the board. Let me just give a few examples:

As I said in my Four Seasons Yachts review, while we had an amazing time, we had way more service issues than I’d consider to be acceptable, given the price point. This was exactly the opposite, and it was just flawless service experience after flawless service experience. So while I’m sure service is consistently good, I’m sure the empty sailing also contributed to taking this to the next level.

We were definitely on an odd sailing, in terms of seasonality, since we were on the second to last voyage before the ship sailed across the Atlantic, to start the winter season in the Caribbean.

Our sailing was empty, with just 19 of the 54 suites occupied, so there were fewer than 40 guests. It really felt like having a private yacht, as we rarely saw others, and we’d go to restaurants for dinner, at most a handful of other tables would be occupied.

On our sailing, almost everyone seemed to be a European retiree, so it was maybe in line with what you’d expect from the stereotypical guest profile of Orient Express trains. However, Ford has had some clients on Orient Express Sailing Yachts, and based on the feedback he has gotten, the ship can be an absolute scene, with some pretty over-the-top people.

The guest profile that Orient Express Sailing Yachts gets is probably a bit different than almost any other cruise line. For one, the ship has already been chartered multiple times in its first season, so you can imagine the kinds of people we’re talking about. And even on sailings that haven’t been chartered, there have been some A-list people onboard.

So anyway, we had a very pleasant, understated crowd onboard, but I’ve also heard the crowd can make for quite some people watching, especially for sailings in the South of France, etc.

As I said at the beginning, my goal here is to be as objective as possible, so what feedback do I have? Honestly, as much as I have a critical eye, I think there are shockingly few areas for improvements. Here are the things that stood out to me:

I also want to acknowledge that Trek Trendy had published a review of the Orient Express Corinthian, and I think that’s worth watching for a different perspective. I think he was being totally fair with some of his critique, but I had a different experience:

I travel a ton, and as much as I have so many amazing experiences, I’m almost always excited to go home, given that I miss family, and travel is sort of my “job.” I have to be honest, the Orient Express Corinthian was the first time in recent memory where I thought to myself “man, I wish it weren’t over.”

Earlier this year I experienced Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection and Four Seasons Yachts, and they’re both great in their own ways. However, Orient Express Sailing Yachts is really in a different league. Yes, it’s priced at the top end of the market, but it also includes the most, and I really appreciate that. There’s something nice about paying a high voyage cost in advance, but then feeling like everything is included.

Orient Express Sailing Yachts really is an unbelievable product, from the design of the ship, to the incredible restaurant and bar concepts, to the service. If you can swing it — and especially if you’ve never taken a cruise before — I can’t recommend this enough.

What’s your take on the Orient Express cruise concept?

#6113. Marriott Bonvoy Elite Status Soft Landings For 2027: Drop Only One Tier

Marriott Bonvoy has just revealed its status soft landing policy for the next membership year, and it’s good news (well, at least for those who don’t requalify for their current status tier).

Marriott Bonvoy has just revealed its status soft landing policy for the 2027 status year, for situations where someone doesn’t qualify for a particular elite tier based on their activity in 2026. Specifically, elite members who don’t achieve the published criteria to maintain their status will only drop down at most one elite tier.

In other words, Ambassador Elites will at most drop to Titanium Elite, Titanium Elites will at most drop to Platinum Elite, Platinum Elites will at most drop to Gold Elite, and Gold Elites will drop at most to Silver Elite.

For what it’s worth, this policy matches Marriott’s historical approach to status soft landings. Before Marriott and Starwood merged, back when Marriott’s loyalty program was named Marriott Rewards, Marriott consistently had a status soft landing policy. With this, Marriott Rewards members never dropped more than one elite tier per year, regardless of their activity.

That policy has continued since the new program was formed, including for the next year. However, there’s no guarantee this will continue to be the policy in the future. For those curious, the status offered as part of the soft landing also does count toward lifetime elite status. So if you’re downgraded from Titanium to Platinum based on a soft landing, that year of Platinum will add to your total.

During the pandemic, we saw airline and hotel loyalty programs largely extend elite status several times. This made sense, given the extent to which business travel decreased for many. However, with the huge increase in leisure travel and all the new ways to earn elite status, we’ve seen elite ranks swell.

Personally I think the concept of a status soft landing makes a lot of sense. After all, sometimes life conditions change for people, and in many cases those changes are just temporary. If you drop from top tier status to no status, you don’t really have much of an incentive to stay loyal to that hotel group when your travel picks up again.

By offering a soft landing, loyalty programs can try to build more of a long term relationship with members, and that’s a positive. We also see some programs allow members to pause their status for a year or extend status as a one-time exception based on life circumstances, and I think that’s a great policy as well.

Marriott Bonvoy has a generous status soft landing policy for 2027, for those who don’t requalify for status in 2026. If you didn’t requalify for your current status tier with Marriott Bonvoy in 2026, you can expect that you’ll be downgraded at most one status level.

What do you make of Marriott Bonvoy’s soft landing policy for status?

#6112. Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

“The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

At issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”

The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

Advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly said it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

Senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

“Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

“Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most important stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”

The House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the issue.

“Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”

#6111. Chase Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card Review: Are The Benefits Worth The Fee?

The Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card is one of the most compelling co-branded airline credit cards out there. I’m a huge fan of the Air Canada Aeroplan program — even if you have no connection to Air Canada or Aeroplan, the program is fantastic for partner redemptions, and this card is worth being aware of. And if you do fly Air Canada with any frequency, the perks for travel on the airline are strong.

So this post is my in-depth Air Canada Aeroplan Card review. Let’s go over all the details, and discuss if the card is worth it.

Link: Learn more about the Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card

Before I review the Air Canada Aeroplan Card benefits in detail, here’s a high-level look at everything you need to know about the card:

Here are my thoughts on the Air Canada Aeroplan Card’s biggest pros and cons:

If you’re thinking about applying for the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card, you’re probably most interested in the welcome bonus it’s currently offering, along with its annual fee and general eligibility rules for getting the card. So let’s get into those details.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card currently has the following welcome bonus: Limited Time Offer: Earn up to 80,000 bonus points. Earn 60,000 bonus points after you spend $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months your account is open. Plus, up to 20,000 more bonus points by earning 50% more bonus points per $1 spent on purchases that normally earn 1 bonus point in the first 2 months from account opening..

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Aeroplan points to be worth 1.4 cents each. That means the 80,000 points are worth $1,120 to me. However, even if you have a different valuation of these points than I do, you can at least use the “Pay Yourself Back” feature to redeem these points for 1.25 cents each toward a travel purchase, so that’s a pretty high “cash out” value.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card is issued by Chase, and has pretty standard application restrictions:

While Chase doesn’t have a public credit score requirement for the Air Canada Aeroplan Card, you’ll have the best chances of approval if your score is in the good range or higher. That roughly translates to a minimum score of 670. However, people have been approved with lower scores and rejected with higher scores, as it’s one of only many factors that determine card eligibility.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card has a $195 annual fee. There’s no cost to add authorized users to the card, and their spending will count toward your points balance and any spending thresholds.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s a great card to use globally, and possibly even earn bonus rewards on your spending depending on what you’re using the card for.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Card has a well rounded rewards structure, among the most interesting you’ll find on any airline credit cards. This isn’t just about the number of points that you earn, but also about the additional rewards for spending. Specifically, the Aeroplan Card offers the following:

Those are some excellent bonus categories. For what it’s worth, the card offers 1x Aeroplan points on all other purchases, so there are better cards for everyday spending.

There’s a lot to love about Air Canada Aeroplan points, even if you don’t usually fly Air Canada or travel to Canada. Among other things:

I redeem miles through Aeroplan all the time, and consistently get great value. Booking award flights on Air Canada itself rather than other partners isn’t always the best deal, though, especially if you’re booking during a peak travel time, since Air Canada awards use dynamic pricing.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Card gives cardmembers plenty of opportunities to earn elite status with Air Canada Aeroplan. You get some status outright just for being a cardmember, and you can earn further status with spending.

Those who are approved for the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card receive Aeroplan 25K status. This is valid for as long as your account is open. Aeroplan Elite 25K is Air Canada’s entry level status, and includes travel perks with Air Canada, including:

Each year, those with the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card also receive 5,000 Status Qualifying Credits (SQCs) to help work toward the next level of Aeroplan status. This is automatic, but as I’ll cover below, you can stack additional credits on top through hitting certain spending thresholds in the calendar year.

For those curious, below are the Aeroplan elite requirements.

Beyond the automatic 5,000 SQCs you’ll receive each calendar year just for having the Air Canada Aeroplan Card, you can earn up to 20,000 additional credits by hitting spending thresholds. Here’s how that breaks down:

So you can earn a total of 25,000 SQCs each calendar year through the Air Canada Aeroplan Card.

Whether or not that’s worth it really depends on how much you fly Air Canada, and what the opportunity cost of your credit card spending is.

Those with the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card can get a one-tier status upgrade to Aeroplan 35K status when they spend $75,000 on the card in a calendar year. You’ll get status for the remainder of the calendar year you qualify and the entire following calendar year.

If you ask me, the value here is really for someone who is actually loyal to Air Canada. Aeroplan 35K status gets you three complimentary checked bags on Air Canada flights (vs. just one with Aeroplan 25K), 10 eUpgrade credits, and a 3x elite points multiplier on eligible Air Canada or Star Alliance flight bookings, among other things.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers a variety of valuable benefits and credits, beyond the elite status perks covered above. Some of these benefits are offered just for being a cardmember, while others can be earned with spending. The perks are pretty comprehensive, and you’ll find almost everything you could want short of lounge access. So let’s go over those.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers up to $100 in Air Canada statement credits when you make qualifying Air Canada purchases. The credits apply to paid airfare, taxes and fees on award flights, and inflight food and drinks, though onboard Wi-Fi is excluded.

This breaks down as two credits of up to $50 each, one from January 1 through June 30 and one from July 1 through December 31. If you book cash fares on Air Canada twice a year, this is an easy way to put $100 back in your pocket, and this benefit alone can cover about half of the card’s annual fee.

As an Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card holder, you can receive a 15% discount on the Aeroplan points required to book an award flight on Air Canada, Air Canada Express, or Air Canada Rouge. In practice, this also seems to work on partner award flights, as long as at least one segment is on Air Canada. The upside here can be absolutely huge, and it’s a great reason to have this card.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers a free first checked bag on Air Canada flights for the primary cardmember and up to eight others traveling on the same itinerary. This applies to itineraries with Air Canada, Air Canada Rouge, or Air Canada Express. The value of that could add up pretty quickly. There’s no need to actually pay for the ticket with the card, as long as you’re the primary cardmember and have your Aeroplan number linked to the reservation.

Once every four years, the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers a credit that’s valid toward a membership with Global Entry, TSA PreCheck, or NEXUS, worth up to $120. These are all programs that can save travelers time at the airport, and potentially even at the border.

I specifically love that the card also offers a NEXUS credit, since that’s historically something we haven’t seen card issuers offer. NEXUS is arguably the best of the three programs, since it gets you access to Global Entry, TSA PreCheck, and expedited immigration in Canada.

Admittedly this is probably more interesting in theory than in practice, but I still like where Aeroplan is going with this. Those with the Air Canada Aeroplan Card will automatically have carbon offsets purchased for their flights when redeeming Aeroplan points for an Air Canada flight.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card is a World Elite Mastercard, which comes with certain perks, including a concierge service and presale tickets for eligible events.

While you’ll want to consult the cardmember agreement for full details, the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers a variety of travel protection when paying with the card, including the following:

There’s another feature that you’ll find on the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card, which isn’t available on any other airline card. Specifically, the Aeroplan Credit Card offers a Pay Yourself Back feature, whereby cardmembers can apply their Aeroplan points toward travel purchases on any airline, hotel, or rental car, at the rate of 1.25 cents per point, up to 200,000 points per year.

This is an incredibly innovative concept, and something that cardmembers may find to be valuable. So whether you want to redeem your points for a stay at a Four Seasons or a flight on JetBlue, the possibilities are endless. It’s also a reason to potentially think of the welcome bonus differently — the bonus points earned with the welcome offer can over time be redeemed toward any recent purchase or even toward the card’s annual fee.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card also offers the ability to earn priority reward vouchers. Each can be used to get 50% off an eligible Aeroplan award ticket, and is valid for travel on Air Canada or a partner airline.

You earn these vouchers at the following four annual spending thresholds:

These can each be used in the same way, and the value depends on your status:

As you can tell, the value here will depend on your status and travel patterns, but there’s potentially quite a bit of value to be had.

While this is something that most people won’t be able to achieve, I love the concept behind this, and for some it might just be the best deal in travel. The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers what I’d consider to be the world’s most valuable companion certificate, for those who spend a million dollars per year on the card.

If you reach that threshold, you’ll receive an award redemption companion voucher that’s valid globally:

We’ve never seen a credit card offer a perk quite this valuable before. Obviously, the spending requirement is massive here, and this would only make sense if you were planning a lot of travel in a particular year. For a certain type of consumer, though, this is an incredible opportunity.

A few Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card benefits are set to expire on December 31, 2026, so they won’t be around for too much longer. Here’s a quick look:

If you already have the card, now is your last chance to take advantage of these perks. Especially with the 10% transfer bonus, it’s worth seeing if an Aeroplan award flight makes sense with your upcoming travel plans so you can get some extra value for your rewards before this perk retires.

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card is an innovative product with a big welcome bonus, great return on spending, and valuable perks. That’s just about all that I look for in a credit card.

Airline co-brand credit cards are extremely popular given the allegiance many people have to a particular airline. Admittedly Aeroplan is at a disadvantage in the US market, since not as many people in the US are loyal to Air Canada as they are to American, Delta, or United, for example.

That being said, I think the thoughtful value proposition of this card more than makes up for it for Air Canada loyalists. If you like to redeem points for international premium cabin awards, it could be worth applying for this card. Similarly, the card can be worth it for the Pay Yourself Back feature, whereby you can redeem your Aeroplan points however you’d like toward a travel purchase.

Hopefully most people find value beyond just the bonus, given the excellent rewards structure.

Arguably the biggest challenge with the Aeroplan Credit Card is how easy Aeroplan points are to earn with other cards that provide more flexibility. Aeroplan is transfer partners with several bank currencies, including Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Chase Ultimate Rewards, and all those currencies can be converted at a 1:1 ratio.

That means the points are pretty easy to come by, and in many cases there are compelling value propositions on those cards as well.

If you’re under 5/24, consider these two cards from Chase:

If you’re over 5/24, these are some other top Aeroplan Card alternatives to consider:

The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card is phenomenal, and easily the most innovative co-branded airline credit card we’ve seen. The card offers a nice welcome bonus, a lucrative rewards structure with a variety of incentives for spending, and comes with great perks, like elite status.

The Aeroplan program is rewarding in general, but if you don’t fly Air Canada or book award flights through Aeroplan more than once or twice a year, you might want to consider earning flexible points that transfer to this program instead.
