The right travel credit card is important for any trip, as it can earn points or miles and provide valuable travel protections. But when you travel for months at a time, other factors — including no foreign transaction fees, international acceptance and benefits you can use outside the U.S. — become especially important.

Living and working on the road without a permanent home base puts these priorities to the test. The best card benefits solve practical problems and remain useful long after a typical vacation would have ended.

With that in mind, these are some of the best cards for long-term travelers and digital nomads.

Now, let's dive into what each of these cards has to offer.

All of the welcome bonus valuations in this guide are based on TPG's November 2026 valuations.

The is best for long-term travelers who want broad travel protections, premium lounge access and flexible points in one card.

Welcome bonus: Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve is an excellent card for long-term travelers because it earns at least 4 points per dollar spent on flights and hotels booked directly and 3 points per dollar spent on dining purchases.

The card's up-to-$300 annual travel credit is straightforward to use, while Chase Sapphire and Priority Pass lounge access can provide a place to work, eat and recharge between flights. The card also charges no foreign transaction fees.

Its travel protections are another reason why it's a great choice for digital nomads. Baggage delay coverage, for example, can help cover essentials when your checked bag doesn't arrive on time. Trip delay and trip cancellation/interruption coverage can also soften the financial hit when plans unravel.

Plus, Chase Sapphire Reserve cardholders can transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to hotel and airline partners, including fan favorites like United MileagePlus and World of Hyatt.

However, the card carries a $795 annual fee, and several of its statement credits are tied to particular merchants.

Cardholders can get up to $500 in statement credits each calendar year for qualifying prepaid stays of at least two nights through The Edit by Chase Travel℠, with a maximum of $250 per transaction. It can be a fantastic perk when a long trip calls for a comfortable hotel reset between apartment stays or after a long-haul flight.

If you spend most of the year outside the U.S., weigh the $795 annual fee against the benefits you’ll use regularly.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

The is best for digital nomads who can use its extensive lounge network, hotel elite status and premium perks.

Welcome bonus: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 175,000 Membership Rewards Points after spending $12,000 on purchases within the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

The Amex Platinum comes offers one of the largest airport lounge networks available. The American Express Global Lounge Collection includes access to Centurion Lounges and participating Priority Pass lounges (enrollment required for Priority Pass Select).

That pairs nicely with a high earning rate on flights booked directly with the airline as well as up to a $200 airline fee statement credit every calendar year on your selected qualifying airline (enrollment required; terms apply).

Cardmembers can transfer their Membership Rewards points to Amex's airline and hotel partners, opening up award flights and hotel stays worldwide.

Several other card benefits lend themselves nicely to travelers who stay in hotels, rather than long-term rentals. Hotel elite status, including Hilton Honors Gold Elite, Leaders Club Sterling and Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite, can make your stays more comfortable (enrollment required).

The up-to-$600 annual lodging statement credit adds more value to the card and can give you an excuse to add luxe stays to your itinerary. It is split into two up to $300 semiannual credits and applies to qualifying prepaid Airbnb Luxe, Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection bookings through American Express Travel®. (Airbnb Luxe and THC require a minimum two-night stay; FHR will also require a minimum two-night stay beginning Jan. 1, 2027; terms apply).

It's worth noting that you likely won't be able to use every statement credit. Someone spending a lot of time outside the U.S. may have trouble using several U.S.-focused perks, including Uber Cash (for U.S. Uber rides and Uber Eats orders) and Walmart+.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Platinum.

The Venture X is best for digital nomads who want premium travel perks and simple rewards on everyday spending.

Welcome bonus: Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

For digital nomads, the Venture X works well because of how little strategy it requires, at home or abroad. It earns 2 miles per dollar spent on purchases outside bonus categories. These flat-rate, hassle-free rewards are useful when your spending habits change from one country to the next.

The card allows you to transfer your miles to 15-plus airline and hotel partners. That's even more flexibility when your travels take you all over the world.

The card's $300 annual Capital One travel credit and 10,000 anniversary miles (worth $100 toward bookings made through the Capital One Travel portal) are very easy ways to offset the annual fee.

Primary cardholders also receive complimentary access to Capital One Lounges, Capital One Landings and participating Priority Pass lounges.

The card offers cellphone protection when you pay your monthly wireless bill with it (up to $800 per eligible claim, with a $50 deductible and a maximum of two claims per 12-month period). That's useful when your phone is your boarding pass, map and connection to work.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture X.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card

The offers a useful middle ground for digital nomads who want strong everyday rewards without paying a hefty annual fee.

Welcome bonus: Earn 60,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months.

At $95 a year, the Strata Premier is the easiest card on this list to justify. Its protections are particularly practical when you live out of a suitcase. The card's 24-month extended warranty can be especially useful when living on the road, as nomadic life can take a toll on electronics and other gear.

Cardholders can transfer ThankYou points to more than 20 airline and hotel partners. There's also an annual $100 hotel benefit per calendar year for a single hotel stay (of $500 or more; excluding taxes and fees) booked through CitiTravel.com or by calling Citi. That's a fast way to offset the card's $95 annual fee.

The Strata Premier offers fewer statement credits than pricier cards. Its $95 annual fee makes it a good fit if you’re traveling on a budget or want an affordable second card.

To learn more, read our full review of the Citi Strata Premier.

The is best for everyday spending abroad, thanks to its earning rate on eligible foreign transactions.

Welcome bonus: Earn 80,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening.

For digital nomads, the card's value comes from a benefit that applies well beyond Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines flights. Cardholders earn 3 Atmos Rewards points per dollar spent on foreign transactions, whether that's a hotel stay, meal, pharmacy visit or souvenir.

You'll also get a 10% rewards bonus on points earned from card purchases if you have an eligible Bank of America account.

Atmos Rewards points can be redeemed for flights on Oneworld carriers and other airline partners, in addition to Alaska and Hawaiian.

The annual Global Companion Award provides a 25,000-point discount when two travelers book award travel on the same itinerary. Based on our valuations, this benefit alone is worth $400. That's enough to justify the annual fee, even if you never touch the other Alaska or Hawaiian-specific benefits.

Cardholders who spend $60,000 in a card anniversary year can earn an additional Global Companion Award worth up to 100,000 points. Since these awards can be used in any class of service, the larger award could be particularly valuable for a premium-cabin or long-haul partner redemption.

That same $60,000 in spending earns 30,000 status points. Combined with the 10,000 status points awarded after each account anniversary, you'd have enough for Atmos Gold status (mapped to Oneworld Sapphire). On eligible itineraries, that's good for business-class lounge access — even when you're flying economy — priority check-in and boarding, preferred seating and extra baggage.

To learn more, read our full review of the Atmos Summit card.

Many long-term travelers and digital nomads run businesses from the road. These travelers may find it useful to have one or more business cards as well.

One business card that's particularly well-suited to this lifestyle is the (see rates and fees).

This card earns 3 points per dollar spent on travel, shipping, social media and search engine advertising, and cable, internet and phone services (on the first $150,000 in combined purchases each account anniversary year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

The Ink Business Preferred also offers cellphone insurance, primary rental car insurance on business-related rentals and no foreign transaction fees.

To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Preferred.

When you live out of a suitcase, the best card benefits aren't always flashy. What matters is what follows you: protections when your laptop dies or your flight gets canceled, solid rewards on everyday spending in any currency and lounges in the airports you actually pass through.

A long list of statement credits might only be great if you'll be back home in a few days. For extended travel, it's more important to pick the card that works wherever you wake up tomorrow.

#6108. KLM Offloaded A Passenger Rather Than Use The Blocked Seat We Offered

I recently flew KLM from Amsterdam to Barcelona, and a passenger was taken off our full flight even though my wife and I offered him the empty seat between us. The crew followed a rule exactly, and as far as I can tell, nobody got anything out of it.

Business class inside Europe is basically a regular economy seat with the middle seat blocked. On some planes the middle seat is physically blocked with a small table. On this flight it was just empty, blocked online so nobody could book it, but technically a regular seat anyone could sit in.

I was on KL1519 on 2 September, in row 2 with my wife, with that empty middle seat between us.

After the doors closed, it turned out that two passengers had boarding passes for the same seat. Whoever got there first sat down. The other one was a fairly young guy, and now he had nowhere to sit. The flight was completely full, there wasn’t a single free seat in economy.

I heard the crew apologizing to him and saying they would have to take him off the plane and put him on the next flight.

I knew this would take a while, because the doors were already closed and he had boarded. Getting him off meant opening the doors again, and maybe taking his bag off too. Once on another flight someone got off and everyone had to hold up their bags.

And I felt sorry for the guy. Maybe he was in a hurry to get somewhere, and none of this was his fault. The airline gave two people boarding passes for one seat, and he was already on board.

So I asked my wife if she minded giving up the empty seat between us. The flight is only about two hours. She was fine with it, so I went to the crew and offered it.

The crew was very grateful, but said seating someone there was against the rules and they couldn’t decide it themselves, they had to check with someone.

That took about 10 minutes. Then they came back, thanked me again, and said that unfortunately it wasn’t possible under the rules.

So they opened the doors and offloaded the guy, I hope they rebooked him on the next one. In the end we pushed back about 40 minutes late and landed in Barcelona about half an hour late. After landing I think even the captain came over, shook my hand and thanked me.

As I understand it, the middle seat is blocked to give the business class passengers more space. In this case that was us, and we were the ones offering to give that space up.

We didn’t need the space, and we’d have put up with one more person in the row for two hours.

On a completely full KLM flight, two passengers got boarding passes for the same seat. My wife and I offered the empty blocked seat between us in business, so he wouldn’t have to get off. The crew checked with someone, the answer was no, and he was offloaded anyway, and we left about 40 minutes late.

I get that the crew couldn’t make this call themselves. Still, we didn’t need that seat at all.

Is there a good reason for this rule that I’m missing?

#6106. Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.

Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

“I think it’s outrageous,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking important.”

Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

"This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he said on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”

But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”

In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson said Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”

Johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he said.

There is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson said Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a plan in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

Senators on both sides of the aisle said they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

“I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability issue, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” said Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

#6105. Malaysia Airlines Orders Up To 16 Boeing 787-10s, Deliveries Start 2032

Malaysia Airlines has just placed a new aircraft order, as the airline will be adding a new wide body aircraft type to its fleet. This seems logical enough, even if the carrier’s long haul fleet seems rather diversified at this point.

Malaysia Airlines has placed its first-ever Dreamliner order, as the airline will be taking delivery of up to 16 Boeing 787-10s. This includes a firm order for 10 jets, plus options for six more, with deliveries expected between 2032 and 2035.

For context, the 787-10 is the largest variant of the Dreamliner. While it has the least range of any 787 variant, the per-seat economics are great, given how it’s “stretched.” While some airlines have started to use the 787-10 for high capacity regional routes, Malaysia Airlines is taking a different approach.

The oneworld carrier intends to use these planes to support its long haul fleet modernization and international expansion, including routes to Europe, along with destinations throughout Asia-Pacific. The airline points out how long haul demand to and from Southeast Asia has increased by more than 50% over the past decade.

Here’s how Malaysia Airlines Group CEO Nasaruddin Bakar describes this:

“The acquisition of the 787 Dreamliner represents a strategic investment in the future of Malaysia Aviation Group. As we look ahead to the next phase of growth, these aircraft will strengthen our ability to serve key international markets with greater capacity, efficiency and flexibility, while delivering the elevated travel experience our customers expect. Beyond fleet renewal, this investment reinforces our commitment to maintaining a modern, competitive airline that supports Malaysia’s connectivity and global aspirations.”

For context, Malaysia Airlines currently has a fleet of just over 90 aircraft, with another 75 aircraft on firm order. As it stands, Malaysia Airlines has:

Now the airline has the following planes on firm order:

A few things stand out here. First of all, it’s cool to see Malaysia Airlines growing again, after a rather rough… what, nearly 15 years? At this point the airline has enough planes on order to both replace its previous generation fleet, and expand. I’d expect the 16 A330ceos will be retired at some point in the coming years, and more than replaced by the A330neos that remain on order. Furthermore, the 737-800s will all be replaced by the 737 MAXs.

The 787-10 is an incredible plane in terms of economics, especially as Boeing has been able to make incremental range improvements, turning it into a true long haul aircraft.

At the same time, I can’t help but feel like it’s unusual how the airline has just seven A350s, with no more on order, and is now switching to the 787 for fleet renewal. Admittedly the A350 was ordered back in the day under a completely different management team, which also at one point thought the A380 was a good fit for the airline.

So I am curious how the carrier’s fleet evolves. Will the seven A350s stick around, or will they eventually just be replaced by 787-10s? Even with airspace restrictions and headwinds, it seems like all of Malaysia Airlines’ routes should be within range for the 787-10, though admittedly London (LHR) might be on the cusp, depending on how airspace closures evolve, how dense of a configuration the airline selects, etc.

The big challenge with the airline industry is that it’s never static, and decisions aren’t made in a vacuum. One management team makes one decision, and then a management team later on can’t just undo what the other management team did, without it being costly. So I get that they’re doing what they can…

Malaysia Airlines is the newest customer for the Boeing 787, as the airline has ordered up to 16 787-10s, including 10 firm orders and six options. The airline plans to use this for a long haul expansion to Europe, as well as for flights in Asia-Pacific.

It’s cool to see Malaysia Airlines continuing to grow, as the carrier has quite the order book at this point. I am curious if the airline keeps around the seven A350s in the long run, or how the airline manages its three wide body aircraft types.

What do you make of Malaysia Airlines’ Boeing 787-10 order?

#6104. SkyWest Pilots Do The Right Thing At SFO, Then Get Snapped At By ATC

With the number of close calls we see at airports nowadays, it’s great to see when pilots or air traffic controllers go above and beyond to be observant, and exhibit good situational awareness. So along those lines, here’s a case of a pilot paying close attention to ensure everyone’s safety, and then an air traffic controller being frustrated by that…

YouTube channel You can see ATC has the air traffic control audio and a visualization of an interaction that happened shortly before noon on November 21, 2026, at San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

In this interaction, a SkyWest Embraer E175 operating on behalf of American Eagle had just landed on runway 28L, after flying from Los Angeles (LAX). The pilots were switched to the ground frequency, and that’s when things quickly went downhill:

The SkyWest pilots then continued their taxi, and when they got to the gate, the conversation continued:

When you screw up, I suppose it’s human nature to get a bit defensive, and I think that’s exactly what happened here.

Credit to the SkyWest pilots for their situational awareness here. They were instructed to taxi in front of another plane, and another plane was instructed to give way to them, but never read back those instructions. The air traffic controller absolutely should have caught that, and as a pilot, they 100% did the correct thing by noticing the lack of a read back, and erring on the side of caution.

This isn’t just some theoretical risk, but ground collisions are the most common kinds of accidents involving commercial aircraft. Could the SkyWest pilots have said “we’re holding short because the other plane didn’t read back instructions?” Sure, but it seems like the time gap here was a matter of seconds, and they didn’t want to step on the radio calls of another pilot, in case they were going to read back.

What I think is really unprofessional is how the air traffic controller then responded to this:

The pilots of a SkyWest flight decided to hold short of a taxiway after they observed the plane that was supposed to give way to them not reading back the correct instructions. That was absolutely the right move, and the air traffic controller should’ve caught that.

When the pilots explained why they held short, the air traffic controller didn’t respond particularly well. Then when they asked for a phone number, she said the pilots would be talking to someone else, and she clearly wasn’t having it. But then she was also mad when the pilot explained very briefly what was going on, saying the conversation should happen off frequency… a conversation she wasn’t willing to have!

This is a clear situation where you have two very professional pilots, and one very unprofessional air traffic controller.

What do you make of this SFO ATC interaction?

#6103. Why JetBlue Is My Favorite Way To Fly Economy Across The Atlantic

I’ve flown back and forth across the Atlantic dozens of times in all cabins, including many times in economy. JetBlue definitely stands out as being my favorite, and dare I say it, the most premium of all the transatlantic economy flights I’ve experienced.

My most recent trip was from Europe to Boston (BOS) for the opening of JetBlue’s newest BlueHouse location. The airline covered my flights for the event, but had no input in this article. I’d like to share some of the reasons that JetBlue’s transatlantic experience impressed me so much.

Economy class meals can seem like quite the downgrade should one be accustomed to the elevated fare at the pointy end of the plane.

JetBlue currently partners with NYC-based Dig Inn for its transatlantic economy-class meals, and they’re far better than average. They also offer products from a range of interesting brands, rather than just your classic soda labels.

Here’s an example of the drinks menu on my flight from Amsterdam to Boston.

Meals are served in these stylish, reusable, matte-black sealed containers. I’d love to see more airlines do more to reduce their waste like this.

I was very happy with my choice of chicken pesto pasta salad as the main course, accompanied by sides of beet and carrot slaw and snap peas with feta. The fresh, flavorful, yet cold dishes were far better than many of the reheated slop I’ve been served in economy before.

I was equally impressed by the breakfast I had on the morning departure back from Boston to London Heathrow (LHR). I went for the Bubly sparkling water again, as I avoid coffee on a plane unless it’s served as espresso. The stuff they pour out of those vats is pretty much just glorified dirty water.

As far as pre-landing light meals go, this pizza thing was pretty good, too.

In addition to the main meal and pre-landing light bite, JetBlue keeps a well-stocked pantry at the back of the Airbus A321LR.

JetBlue has been offering fast, free, in-flight Wi-Fi for as long as I can remember. The same cannot be said for some full-service carriers, which still can’t guarantee a reliable, fast, and free connection on their transatlantic flights.

They’ve also added some fun tech features, like the ability to choose the elements for the main meal service via the IFE screen, even in economy. I think it has a more premium feel than being asked “chicken or beef?”

I’m not a frequent JetBlue flyer, so I couldn’t really make the most of the fun personalization features, such as the option to continue watching the movie where you left off on your last flight.

Being given anything more than the standard pillow and blanket in economy is a rare bonus. It had been so long since my last JetBlue flight in economy that I’d forgotten about the complimentary Snooze Kit.

I prefer to use my AirPods to earplugs, but I did make good use of the eye mask for a mid-flight nap.

I’ve flown over my fair share of narrow bodies on long-haul flights, and I genuinely don’t know why such a fuss is made about them being terrible.

JetBlue’s version of the aircraft has comfy seats, with standard Core (economy) seats having 32 inches of pitch. Another common complaint I hear is that there are fewer toilets. For a plane with far fewer passengers (only 114 in economy), fewer toilets kind of makes sense. I didn’t once find myself waiting in line to use the bathroom on either flight.

For what it’s worth, there are two lavatories for 114 economy passengers, so that’s one lavatory per 57 passengers. That’s a little lower than the industry standard, but not by much. For example, American’s standard 787-9s have five lavatories for 255 economy seats, so that’s a ratio of one lavatory per 51 passengers.

If you’ve only got the budget or the points for economy for your next trip to Europe, I couldn’t recommend JetBlue more. They now fly to eight cities in Europe, the planes are comfortable and modern, and the in-flight food and beverage is top of the game for economy.

What do you make of JetBlue’s transatlantic economy offering?

#6100. British Airways Visa Card Review: Is It Worth The $95 Annual Fee?

The British Airways Visa Signature® Card is one of Chase’s co-branded airline credit cards, and British Airways Club is certainly a popular frequent flyer program, given the overall value of the Avios ecosystem, plus the number of destinations in the United States that British Airways serves.

Who should be applying for the British Airways Visa, and under what circumstances is it worth spending money on it? Let’s take a look at what you need to know about this card, and what the best alternatives are.

Link: Learn more about the British Airways Visa Signature® Card

Before jumping into a closer look at every aspect of the British Airways Visa Card, here’s a high-level view of the card’s key features, perks, and fees:

Here are my thoughts on the biggest British Airways Visa Card pros and cons:

If you’re considering the British Airways Visa Signature Card, its welcome bonus, application rules, and annual fee are all probably top of mind. So let’s start by taking a look at these important details.

The British Airways Visa currently offers the following welcome bonus: Earn 75,000 Avios after you spend $5,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

Based on my current points and miles valuations, which put Avios at 1.2 cents apiece, this current bonus is worth about $900. That’s a pretty solid welcome bonus, especially for a card with a moderate annual fee.

The British Airways Visa has a $95 annual fee. This is not waived for the first year, and there’s no additional fee to add authorized users.

British Airways’ credit card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s potentially a great card to use for purchases abroad.

The welcome bonus on the British Airways Visa isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months. You are eligible for this card if you’ve had the Iberia Visa Signature® Card and/or Aer Lingus Visa Signature® Card, despite the similarities between the cards.

Chase’s other general policies on card approvals apply as well, including the 5/24, whereby you generally won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more credit cards in the last 24 months.

The British Airways Visa Card has no foreign transaction fees, but does the rewards structure warrant putting spending on the card? It might, but only thanks to additional bonuses offered by the card, which incentivize spending.

The British Airways Visa doesn’t have terribly exciting bonus categories. You earn:

There are lots of great credit cards for airfare purchases and hotel purchases. This isn’t a card I would be putting much spending on unless you’re trying to earn a Travel Together Ticket, in which case it could definitely be worth it. More on that below.

British Airways Club is a transfer partner of Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Chase Ultimate Rewards, so it could make sense to put spending on a card earning one of those currencies if you want to earn Avios at an accelerated rate.

There are lots of great uses of British Airways Avios. British Airways Club has roughly distance based award pricing, and the program offers value in situations where other programs might not. Generally speaking, here’s where I see value with Avios:

British Airways is known for adding large taxes and surcharges to some of its own award flights, so this is worth keeping in mind.

Personally I find Avios to be one of the most useful frequent flyer programs for redeeming points, thanks to the number of redemptions this opens up.

Often one of the big challenges people have with points is figuring out how to pool them since you typically need enough points in a single account for a redemption. A cool feature of the British Airways Club program is that you can form household accounts. This allows you to pool the Avios you earn with up to six other people registered at the same address as you.

This is especially awesome in the context of a credit card welcome bonus, since you can pool a ton of Avios in a single account if you have two people get the card in a household, etc.

There are some benefits to the British Airways Visa Card that could alone justify having this card. For some people, it will be worth spending money on the card to unlock some perks, while for others just having the card and not spending money on it offers sufficient benefits. Let’s look at what those benefits are, and how they work.

One of the best benefits of the British Airways Signature Visa is that it offers a 10% discount on British Airways flights starting in the United States. To take advantage of this, just book through ba.com/chase10, and use your card to pay while using promotion code BACHASE10.

If you fly British Airways with any frequency, this could cover the annual fee over and over. See this post for everything you need to know about the British Airways Visa flight discount.

If you have the British Airways Visa Card and redeem Avios for a reward flight, you can receive up to $600 in statement credits annually. You can earn up to three statement credits, as follows:

There are some basic terms to be aware of:

British Airways now also offers Reward Flight Saver from the United States, allowing you to redeem more Avios and pay lower surcharges. Getting a further statement credit of up to $200 on that is pretty great.

One of the potentially great perks of the British Airways Visa is that you can earn a Travel Together Ticket when you spend $30,000 on the card in a calendar year.

This companion ticket will be deposited in your British Airways Club account four to six weeks after you’ve completed the required spending.

With this certificate, you can book a British Airways award ticket at the full cost of Avios (plus taxes, fees, and surcharges), and then for the second passenger you don’t have to pay any Avios, but rather just have to pay all the fees.

This also offers a lot of flexibility — you can also use the voucher as a solo traveler and get 50% off the Avios required for a ticket. Your ticket can originate anywhere in the world, and you can even travel on Aer Lingus or Iberia.

This can represent a fantastic deal for first and business class travel, given how much those tickets would otherwise cost. This isn’t for everyone, though it has the potential to represent a good value, and I know it’s a feature that many value.

See this post for everything you need to know about the British Airways Visa companion voucher.

As a Visa Signature card, the British Airways Visa comes with the following shopping and travel protection benefits:

You’ll want to review the card’s benefits guide for any exclusions and rules that apply.

The British Airways Visa Card has a solid welcome bonus, and that could be a legitimate motivator for picking up this card. However, personally this isn’t a card I would use for everyday spending, since you can earn British Airways Avios at a better rate with other American Express or Chase cards. It also lacks a few benefits that many other airline credit cards offer, including a free checked bag and priority boarding.

That said, I absolutely think this card is worth holding onto if you fly British Airways with any frequency because:

There are several Avios currencies, with three belonging to International Airlines Group (IAG) airlines — there’s British Airways, Aer Lingus, and Iberia. There are also two other US-based credit cards that directly earn Avios from these airlines. Specifically, we’re talking about the Iberia Visa Card (learn more) and Aer Lingus Visa Card (learn more).

Which of these cards should you select? They have a lot in common:

The differences mainly come in the form of the perks associated with just holding onto the cards, and also the perks associated with spending $30,000 on the cards in a calendar year:

The best card to select comes down to which benefits you value most. Also, remember that you’re eligible for all three of these cards, should you be interested, so you don’t necessarily have to choose between them.

See here for a full comparison of cards earning Avios.

If you want to earn British Airways Avios, I’d recommend getting a card that earns either Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, or Chase Ultimate Rewards points. Here’s why:

With that in mind, which cards should you consider? Here are some of my favorite Chase Ultimate Rewards-earning cards:

If you’re over 5/24 or simply prefer Amex points or Capital One miles, here are some top choices:

The British Airways Visa is one of the best co-branded airline credit cards out there, in my opinion. The card offers a solid welcome bonus, and it can be worth spending money on the card to earn a companion ticket.

Beyond that, the card can be worth having for the discounts offered on both paid tickets (up to 10% off) or award tickets (up to $200 in statement credits), which can cover the annual fee over and over. That said, the card would be even stronger if it offered a free checked bag and lounge access as benefits — though I’d expect the annual to increase if those were added, especially the latter perk.

When it comes to earning British Airways Avios long term, personally I’d much rather earn Amex, Bilt, Capital One, and Chase points, and transfer them to British Airways. Not only does this allow you to earn points at a much faster rate, but it also gives you a lot more flexibility.

#6099. Norse Atlantic Collapses: Airline Cancels Flights, Strands Passengers

Back in August 2026, all-Boeing 787 airline Norse Atlantic Airways announced it was in a rough financial spot, and was pursuing a sale, merger, or other arrangement. Not a whole lot of progress was made in subsequent months, and just this morning, the airline announced that it was in a “critical” financial situation.

Well, it seems that it didn’t take long for things to get much worse, as the airline has seemingly canceled all flights just hours later, leaving travelers stranded.

Earlier today, Norse Atlantic provided an update on its financial situation and ongoing strategic review. There’s no point in paraphrasing this, so here’s the direct statement from the airline:

The Company’s financial situation is critical. It is dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs and to continue its operations. Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover. In parallel, the Board and management have diligently considered other available options, including ACMI contracts. Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution.

To state the obvious, this sounded really, really bad. When the company was publicly stating that its “financial situation is critical” and that it needed to secure financing to meet “short-term liquidity needs,” you knew things weren’t good. I expected we’d see something bad happen in the coming weeks, but it didn’t take that long.

Norse Atlantic has canceled its own scheduled flights effective immediately. On top of that, the airline was leasing two jets to Pakistan International Airlines, and those flights were also canceled with very little notice, “due to an unexpected operational suspension” by Norse Atlantic. Travelers were literally checking in at the airport when they realized the airline was grounded.

Due to an unexpected operational suspension by our wet-lease partner Norse Air without prior notice, tonight’s PK786 (London–Islamabad) & PK710 (Manchester–Lahore) are cancelled.We deeply regret the disruption. Efforts have been made to mitigate the impact, and from tomorrow,…

So while the company hasn’t formally announced that it’s liquidating, it’s clear that operations are at least suspended, and we’ll see how this all plays out.

The airline industry can be a funny business, and there’s no clearer example of that than Norse Atlantic Airways. The airline launched in 2022, with the goal of operating long haul, low cost flights, particularly across the Atlantic.

That wasn’t exactly a unique business model, because this was exactly what Norwegian did, before it discontinued long haul flights in 2021. Not only was the idea sort of copied, but Norse Atlantic had some executives from Norwegian, and even picked up the planes that Norwegian previously flew.

But as is all too common in the airline industry, clearly they thought it would be different this time around… it wasn’t. So in 2024 we saw the airline update its business model, making the focus less about operating regularly scheduled commercial flights, and more about leasing out aircraft, all while reducing its fleet.

The company got a lifeline when IndiGo decided to lease some Norse Atlantic 787s to dabble in long haul flying, ahead of the airline taking delivery of its own Airbus A350s. However, between all the airspace closures, high oil costs, and generally declining performance at IndiGo as the airline increasingly moved away from its core strengths, the airline recently decided to scrap that experiment, and stop leasing planes from Norse Atlantic.

Since then, opportunities for Norse Atlantic have been limited. The airline did manage to lease a couple of Dreamliners to the “new” Pakistan International Airlines, but for an airline with 12 planes, that hardly pays the bills.

Norse Atlantic did still operate some of its own flights, but in a very limited capacity. The airline had some flights from Europe to Thailand, South Africa, and the United States, but most were seasonal, and they were a fraction of what they previously were. Clearly they just didn’t have enough money to “keep the lights on” anymore.

I am curious to see what comes next for Norse Atlantic’s 787s. The airline doesn’t own them, but instead, they’ll presumably return to their leasing companies. I can’t help but point out that Southwest Airlines wants to start long haul flights. The airline had been considering a Boeing 787 order, and was possibly even looking at ways to get planes faster than from a direct order (which requires waiting for years).

Could these dozen Norse Atlantic 787s somehow end up at Southwest? The interiors would just need some updates (assuming the airline wants to offer business class), but talk about a quick way to grow a decent sized fleet.

This morning, Norse Atlantic released a statement admitting that its “financial situation is critical,” and that the company’s future is “dependent on securing financing to meet short-term liquidity needs.” That wasn’t exactly a great sign, but little did we know that the company would collapse just hours later, as the airline has now ceased all flying, including on a wet lease basis.

Financial issues at the company started when… well, it launched. Norse Atlantic was just a direct replica of Norwegian, which had failed. When the airline realized that the long haul, low cost business model doesn’t really work, they tried to pivot to wet leasing. And while there’s some demand for that, it’s also not a 100% consistent business in terms of demand.

I feel horribly for all the frontline employees at Norse Atlantic who put their best foot forward. May they find good opportunities at other airlines.

What do you make of Norse Atlantic’s seeming collapse?

Doesn't seem like the LCC model works very well for long haul flying. Particularly when margins fluctuate wildlylike this year thanks to the maga war in the middle east. Unfortunate for all the travelers involved, though, and there should be stricter regulation (or other accommodation) for these marginal airlines...

Anyone correct me if I'm wrong, but the customers of PIA stranded on the UK-to-Pakistan flights should be theoretically entitled to UK261 (i.e. £520 pp)

Yet another tombstone on the already overcrowded graveyard of airlines that had tried the longhaul low-cost model and failed.

Not really surprised that many airlines go bust due to fuel prices. But I am suprised that their ACMI operation for PK is first affected. While European bankruptcy laws are usually not as generous for restructuring as Chapter 11 in the US, they usually do require the bankruptcy administrator to safe money if this can be done by continuing (partial) operation. If the ACMI contract with PK was at least recovering the cost, they would have to operate. Or is even this contract loss making ...?

I'm still surprised that e.g. the EU/UK don't have a "last resort" fund to essentially "force" airline operations to continue for 2-3 days in a shutdown situation. It would probably be easier to handle than ATOL/Package Travel Directive rebookings at the last minute. I'd be thinking a day or two at "full" operations and then maybe a few more during a wind-up at partial operations, and then when you're like a week out ATOL/PTD-type cover could manage the remnants more smoothly (since you generally wouldn't be trying to stuff people onto already-packed flights).

#6098. Why Entitlement Reform Is Easier Abroad Than in America

Privatization, among other proposals, requires a particular set of conditions that the U.S. seems to lack.

Pedestrians walk along a street in the Old Town of Stockholm, Sweden, October 17, 2024.

Senator Ron Johnson’s proposal to sustain Social Security payouts even after the projected depletion of its funds in 2032 has attracted new interest in entitlement reform. Fifteen years ago, Paul Ryan became the victim of character assassination over his plans for modest entitlement reforms. In 2005, George W. Bush attempted to reform Social Security, yet his efforts were in vain.

Johnson’s proposal is poorly conceived, even by the low standards of populists. It would set the United States on course to default even faster than it currently is.

John Gustavsson is a writer from Sweden and holds a doctorate in economics. He is Senior Editor of Nation & Citizenship at Restoring the West and a former adviser to the Sweden Democrats in the European Parliament.
